speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF UNITED STATES SENATORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, possibly I can at this time make reference to the fact that in the gallery today there are two representatives of that impressive and powerful legislative body, the United States Senate. I refer to Senator George D. Aiken of Vermont and Senator Homer E. Capehart of Indiana. Both these gentlemen are here in Ottawa to meet with Your Honour and the Speaker of the other place for the purpose of laying the foundation for a joint committee of legislators representative of our two bodies.
I shall say no more than that. We welcome them for the purpose for which they are here. We welcome them as representatives of that great body which has such powerful legislative capacity and ability. We welcome them because they come from our neighbour, the United States of America, whose co-operation and adherence to freedom give hope to all mankind.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF UNITED STATES SENATORS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to join in the welcome the Prime Minister has expressed to the two representatives of the Senate of the United States who are visiting us today, both of whom I had the pleasure of meeting in the happy days when I lived in Washington. They are here on a mission which, if it can be accomplished-and I am sure it can-will make an important contribution to improving, even more, the good relations between our two countries. Their presence here today, Mr. Speaker, also reminds us that the congress of the United States has completed its work.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF UNITED STATES SENATORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the C.C.F. I am very happy to join the Prime Minister and the Leader of the
57071-3-289i
Opposition in welcoming these two distinguished senators from the United States, Senator Aiken of Vermont and Senator Cape-hart of Indiana. I am certain their visit will result in the establishment of the joint Canada-United States committee in such a form as to result in very great benefits to both nations in the years ahead.
I think we all realize that the prosperity of Canada is closely allied to economic conditions in the United States, and we believe that any procedure that will result in increased trade between our nations and a reduction of trade barriers will redound to the benefit of both countries. The Prime Minister has said that our nation, together with the United States, stands solidly for freedom, and we hope this committee will strengthen the processes of freedom in both nations. A few years ago I had the very great honour of being introduced on the floor of the Senate of the United States. Perhaps our procedures are a little more formal, but I know that our sentiments are just as sincere in welcoming wholeheartedly to our gallery these two distinguished senators from our neighbouring nation, the United States of America.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF UNITED STATES SENATORS
speechtext: Perhaps I may be permitted on this occasion to add my own very warm words of welcome, and to assure the house that if by any chance the senators from the United States have not heard the unanimous and warm greetings which have been extended to them, I shall be happy to convey these messages.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday last
I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce if he would care to comment on an Associated Press dispatch to the effect that President Eisenhower was now considering a recommendation that the tariff on lead and zinc imports from Canada into the United States should be raised. The minister said he would have the answer available for the next day- that was Tuesday. I wonder if the minister can now give me a reply.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: LEAD AND ZINC-REPORTED RECOMMENDATION TO RAISE UNITED STATES TARIFF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had the answer ready and I regret that I did not give it to the Leader of the Opposition yesterday. The position in regard to lead and zinc at the present time is as follows. Last April 24 the United States tariff commission recommended that increased tariffs should be imposed on imports of these products into the United States and at that time President Eisenhower deferred his decision on these recommendations pending congressional consideration of legislation that had been proposed to subsidize producers in the United States. On August 21 the United States congress rejected this proposed legislation. In view of this fact the United States administration is now studying what action, if any, it should take with respect to lead and zinc.

As far as the Canadian government's position is concerned, our views have already been expressed to the United States government on several occasions, making it abundantly clear that any increased tariffs or other measures restricting exports of these important products to the United States would be of the most serious concern.

speechtext: Could I ask the minister a supplementary question. Has he made any inquiries or has he received any information with respect to the reported global plan which was mentioned in the United States congress for the allocation of base metal markets among western producers?

speechtext:
That is right. But we went to the trouble of making a transcript of the statement of the Prime Minister as it was actually given over the air. We compared it with the statement that was issued, and there are some differences in the two texts. I am quoting from the transcript we made of the actual words of the Prime Minister, and this is what he said:
Its success will add greatly to the strength of Canada's national economy and all that means to the welfare and security of all our people. It will include the fullest development of our resources. It will mean bigger and better jobs. It will mean a higher standard of living for every Canadian. It will mean the achievement of a great Canada.
And again from the same broadcast:
I ask that all Canadians, and everyone who holds victory bonds, will now reinvest in Canada's future for a further period in order to support a constructive program for the future of Canada, for you and for your children and your children's children.
This is very eloquent but it does not bear much relationship to this particular financial operation. It is a visionary picture to advocate, to justify and, if I may use the expression, to sell to the public what is essentially a refunding operation. The Prime Minister admitted that himself when in his broadcast he also said:
And I should perhaps make it clear that a conversion bond such as this does not involve any new borrowing on the part of the government.
That one short sentence destroys the whole case of the Prime Minister. Since a conversion loan does not involve any new borrowing it does not of itself involve any new investment leading, as the Prime Minister claimed, to the fullest development of our resources, to bigger and better jobs, to a higher standard of living, to the achievement of a great Canada. This conversion operation,

in short, is not even a loan, strictly speaking. It is a refunding of past loans, a conversion of bonds which, in a significant proportion, would not have been maturing for several years, eight years in the case of the longest victory loan, the ninth.
I think, therefore, that the Prime Minister in his broadcast to the nation did not give the real reasons which led the government to undertake this operation at this time. It appears to me that on this occasion at least the Minister of Finance used more sober and sensible words to describe the conversion operation in a statement issued by his department on July 14.

He did not indulge in so much high flown eloquence but he had this to say:
The minister explained that the refinancing plan is primarily aimed at reorganizing the national debt with a view to putting it on a long term basis and reducing for the government the amount of refinancing to be done over the next few years.
In this house on the same day, July 14, the minister stated, as found at page 2203 of Hansard:
This conversion offer will perform the major and essential task of clearing the way for an orderly program of debt management over the years ahead. It will not, however, provide us with any new cash.
That makes it clear, of course, that a conversion operation has no direct relation to new development and contradicts the argument presented by the Prime Minister to the public. The minister, however, at that time and since has been very vague about the basic reasons which caused him to announce this operation. What does he mean, for instance, when he says "this conversion offer will perform the major and essential task of clearing the way for an orderly program of debt management over the years ahead"? Does this orderly program of debt management simply mean that the government is now facing a series of heavy deficits during the years ahead, that its new cash requirements will be very great indeed during those years, and that this conversion offer will perform the major and essential task of clearing the way for meeting a rapid increase in the public debt?
That increase is apparent, Mr. Chairman, in the fact that the government's new cash requirements for this fiscal year alone will exceed $1,400 million. Furthermore, the huge budgetary deficit announced by the minister, which may be greater than announced by him, did not have anything to do with any vision of development or with any so-called special works program. It was largely due to the current recession and the consequent

drop in government revenues and increased long term commitments, especially in the field of social security.
We have been warned by a well known financial economist, Mr. Harvey Perry, whom the minister knows as most of us do, that we might have a series of budgetary deficits until 1967, so the government would have to borrow important amounts each year during that period. Is it because the government accepts this view that it decided suddenly, after the budget was introduced in the house, to launch this conversion operation, thereby clearing the way for new and heavy borrowing in the years ahead?
Surely, Mr. Chairman, even at this late date in the session we are entitled to a sober and clear statement by the minister on the real reasons lying behind this major financial operation, especially after the Prime Minister's attempt on radio and television to dress up this so-called conversion operation in the patriotic colours of wartime emergency and grandiose national development. That is why I wish to ask the minister some questions. Perhaps he will be good enough to reply at the end of the discussion of this item of his estimates or at some time during that discussion convenient to him.
First, what is the cost of the operation? There has been a good deal of speculation about this. I know the difficulties in estimating the cost, but surely the government must now have some rough estimates even though precise figures may not be possible. Second, what is the cost of publicity, and what advertising agencies have been involved? I cannot say that I am much impressed by some of the advertising, especially that full page picture of the old lady with a new hat. It all must have cost a great deal of money and it has introduced, I admit, a new element into government financing in this country.
Mr. Bruce Hutchison had an amusing editorial

more than amusing; very shrewd -in the Victoria Daily Times on this aspect of the matter entitled "The Lady and the Hat." Perhaps the minister has read it. It included the following:
A few years back any government advertisement was a cold, depressing statement of the facts and if it was a fiscal advertisement nobody but a bond dealer or an auditor bothered to read it.
Probably in the minister's eyes that justifies this new kind of advertising.
Now we behold a life-size portrait of a quaint, twinkling lady with a funny hat who, we are told, has just bought one of the new bonds and safely arranged the security of her old age.
Instead of boring us with statistics, the government announces, with a chuckle that the funny hat was bought with the premium on the bond. The lady, the reader, the whole nation is happy.
Supply-Finance
The bond campaign becomes a great lark. Even the grim fiscal visage of Mr. Fleming relaxes as Canada goes deeper into debt.
If high finance is such a jolly pastime why didn't we hear of it before? If debt is so profitable, so kindly to old ladies, by all means let us have more of it.
Well, we are likely to have more of it. That is the second question, the cost of publicity. Third, what is the amount of dealer commissions, bond issuing fees, delivery commission to banks and trust companies? Fourth, what is the total amount of premiums to bondholders? I know the minister cannot give us the exact figures.

speechtext: Premiums?

speechtext:
Total premiums to bondholders; cash bonuses. While the minister may not be able to give us exact figures, surely he can give us same indication of what this is costing the country, especially in the light of reports that have been circulating. I have seen reports in reputable journals, including reputable financial journals, that if this operation is fully successful it will cost as high as $100 million. I have seen reports varying from $70 million to $100 million. Dividing those reports into the categories of costs I have mentioned in my request to the minister, there have been representations that advertising will cost $2 million; that commissions to dealers and agents will cost between $25 million and $50 million. This commission ranges from a quarter of one per cent to one per cent plus a quarter of one per cent bond-issuing fee. I have seen reports that the cash bonuses to holders will be as low as $37 million or as high as $60 million. These bonuses range from 1J per cent to 2i per cent.
Then I want to ask the question, what are the additional interest charges that taxpayers will have to pay, which have been estimated to be as high as $100 million per year for the next 25 years? It depends, of course, on how successful the operation will be, but we learned last Tuesday that $5 billion has been reconverted and most of it, I suppose, into the 25-year bonds. There are only a few days yet to go in this campaign, so the minister should have some reasonably accurate estimates of this.
Then, and this is an important question, perhaps the minister could give us some information on who holds these bonds and who will gain most from the conversion. Dr. Brewis, associate professor of economics at Carleton University, had this to say on this point in an article which I read on July 22:
Only a very small proportion of the victory bonds are held by the man in the street. I do not pretend to know the exact proportion but it could be of the order of 10 or 15 per cent of the whole. The great bulk are known to be held by financial

Sup p ly-Finance
and other institutions and the success of the conversion will depend much more on their actions than on those of the private individual. To the extent moreover that the refunding is successful it will involve a transfer of income in favour of these institutions.
That is a quotation from Dr. Brewis's article. The Bank of Canada made its own breakdown on May 31, so far as the holdings of these bonds are concerned. The figures in that breakdown are as follows: the Bank of Canada, $1,300 million; the unemployment insurance commission, $300 million; the government, $100 million, and the chartered banks, $1,400 million. This gives a total held by the government and the chartered banks of $3,100 million. A leading supporter of the government in the other place raised this figure during a debate there a couple of weeks ago to $3,300 million. This leaves us with something over $3 billion to be accounted for.
What I should like from the minister is how this $3 billion-plus is divided as between institutional holders and private individuals. Again I know he cannot give us exact figures, but surely he must have some estimates of this. Surely he must have had some estimate of this kind of division before deciding on the terms of the loan or the kind of publicity campaign to be waged. Professor Brewis says that only 10 per cent to 15 per cent of this $3 billion is held by individuals.

The professor said it could have been of the order of 10 per cent or 15 per cent. He has made his estimate, and perhaps the minister will give us his. I have seen another estimate that perhaps half this amount would be held by institutions and perhaps half by individuals, which would mean that about $1,550 million would be held by each.
Now, there is certainly little need to try to convince the institutions to convert their bonds. Surely they must have been delighted with this windfall dumped into their laps by a government which told them how patriotic they would be if they accepted it. In order to see what can be the magnitude of the gifts-I use that word because I think it is the correct word-involved in certain individual cases, let us use an illustration which may well correspond to a concrete and real situation. Suppose, for instance, that a life insurance company is holding $40

million of the ninth victory loan bonds which it is converting into the new 25-year bonds. This company, in converting, would receive a cash adjustment of $600,000, plus about 12 per cent of $40 million representing the additional and unexpected interest income for the period until September 1, 1966, when its old bonds would have reached maturity. This means that in this case, hypothetical if you like but not very far from reality, the company would receive as a gift out of this conversion operation an amount exceeding $5 million, or over $600,000 a year for the next eight years.
Well, what about the individuals? If we are to assume, and I do not think it is unreasonable to assume, that half this $3 billion or $1.5 billion is held by individuals, it means that this is the only group at which this high pressure, expensive campaign could have been aimed. I ask the minister, therefore, are the results justifying it in terms of the amount of individual holdings being converted, in view of the amount of money and effort spent on it?
I should like to turn now to another aspect of the question, that is the economic effects of this conversion operation in so far as one is able to determine them. In the course of these remarks I want to ask the minister some more questions. Possibly the most immediate effect will be that interest rates to provincial governments, municipalities and private borrowers will go up. This raises a question which the minister should try to answer or at least give us the benefit of his opinion. Will this conversion cause a rise in long term rates? If so, can we also expect later an increase in short term rates? Will we in this country be in the strange and paradoxical position of having at the same time easy money, in terms of supply, and dear money in terms of interest rates, a result brought about not so much by market forces as by government action? What will be the effect of those higher interest rates during a period not of boom but of pause or recession, in terms of economic stability and prosperity? How will this help to meet mounting unemployment? How and to what extent will these rates contribute to effective control over potential inflationary pressures, and there is no more important aspect of the problem than that? The minister dealt with it at some length, and rightly so, in his broadcast on Tuesday.
Then what is going to happen to the real value of the new bonds? Will it be eroded by the cheating process of inflation over the years? There is another aspect of the question with which the minister should deal. When interest rates are higher in Canada

than in the United States, more Canadians tend to borrow there and more people from the United States tend to lend here, and that pushes our exchange rate up and handicaps our exporters and as well increases import competition in the Canadian market.
I therefore ask the minister a final question on this aspect of the matter. Does he not think that the conversion loan will make interest rates higher in Canada than in the United States, thereby increasing the premium on the Canadian dollar? I am aware of the action taken recently in the United States has brought their interest rates down and in the last few weeks our exchange premium, probably because of that development, has gone down. But does he not think that the long term effect of this conversion, basing our interest rates at 4J per cent, may have the possible effect of increasing the premium on the Canadian dollar?
What we want then, Mr. Chairman, is as full a statement as possible of all the reasons for this unprecedented operation; its advantages and disadvantages; its implications, direct and indirect, on our economy. There can be no intelligent appreciation and no intelligent discussion of the operation without a statement of this kind from the minister.
Finally there is one question I want to ask. I think I said "finally" a moment ago, but I assure the minister that this one is final. Why did the minister not announce this operation in his budget speech? At that time he described the government's borrowing program in the following terms, as found at page 1241 of Hansard:
-during this fiscal year we shall need to sell bonds or other securities in a total amount of close to $3,400 million.
Of this amount $1,400 million was to meet the need for new cash to cover a deficit and $1,950 million to cover the marketable funded debt maturing during this year. Then less than a month later the minister announced the refunding loan amounting not to $1,950 million, as he indicated in his budget speech, but to $6,400 million. Why then did he not make that announcement in his budget, so as to permit us to have a full discussion in the course of that debate? Did he decide on June 17 not to take the house into his confidence then, or did he change his mind after June 17? If so, for what reason? I suggest that those are important questions, Mr. Chairman.
Perhaps in this connection I might quote from an editorial published in the Financial Post on July 19, which included this paragraph:
It Is interesting that this whole plan developed so rapidly. Only a little more than a month ago,
Supply-Finance
the finance minister was talking about refunding on a bit by bit basis. This drastic big clean-up scheme originally evolved in a Toronto financial house, has brought a basic turn-around in government plans.

I am sure the minister will want to clear up that point as well as some of the other points I have mentioned in this statement. For instance, some people would like to know why the minister felt it necessary to refund the eighth victory loan bond issue and the ninth victory loan bond issue at a time when there are still five years and eight years respectively before maturity in the case of these two issues. It has been contended that these bonds had been sold in good faith on terms agreeable to the buyers, to carry interest at 3 per cent to maturity. It has also been alleged that a great proportion of these bonds were held by banks and insurance companies and trust companies, which have agreed to convert them into the new 4-| per cent bonds, thereby receiving a direct bonus plus 1J per cent more in interest per year for eight years in the case of the ninth victory loan bond, which alone represents a total of well over 12 per cent, as I have already stated, at 1J per cent compounded annually for eight years.
We on this side of the house over recent weeks, as I have stated, have done and said nothing to increase any doubts the Canadian public might have as to some features of this conversion loan. In that respect I suggest we have acted responsibly. Even now, with the loan period nearly over, we are not opposing the purposes of this financial operation as an effort in debt management prior to an appeal for more money. Indeed, as I said, we do not have the main pertinent facts which would enable us to take a final position

Supply-Finance
on this issue. However, we blame the government and the Minister of Finance for the present state of confusion and of some suspicion because adequate information has not been made available.
We are now requesting from the minister a full statement on the various features and implications of this huge conversion operation which is of such great immediate as well as long term significance to our economy. Perhaps if the minister had previously answered these questions-most of which, if they have not been raised in the house have been raised by the public and in the press- he would find it less difficult now to fully reach his objective. Perhaps it is not yet too late to provide these answers and ensure the successful completion of this operation which, once it has been decided on, all of us feel should be carried through to a successful conclusion.
Our criticism is that we were not given information on these matters in this house at an earlier time and that many questions are left unanswered, including these questions I have asked, even at this late date in the session. Our criticism is that if these questions had been answered previously the doubts and uncertainty that have arisen might have been removed; that this operation would have been carried on in a better atmosphere than has been the case, and some of these blitz tactics which we read about in the press might not have been necessary. Before the estimate is passed I hope the minister will clear up those points.

I should like to make one or two comments on the subject matter dealt with by the Leader of the Opposition, namely the conversion loan program. I do not think it is necessary at this time for us to go into as much detail as did the Leader of the Opposition, because I and others in the C.C.F. party at a prior time during this session dealt quite extensively with it and laid the groundwork then, by the legitimate complaints we raised, for the comments made by the Leader of the Opposition this morning. Actually all we are doing in the conversion loan program is borrowing money to pay off debts that we incurred by borrowing money in the first place. Incidentally, I may say that borrowing had been done under a Liberal administration.
I listened with a great deal of interest to the comments of the Leader of the Opposition, hoping to hear some new and enlightened approach to the financial problems of this nation but of course my expectations and hopes in that regard were probably not too well founded. After all, we cannot expect much from either the Conservative

party or the Liberal party with respect to a different type of approach to our financial problems and to control of the money system in Canada, because they both endorse the economic system and financial system that operates in this country.
I did hear from the Leader of the Opposition a sort of simulated angered condemnation coupled with what was actually an en-dorsation of that program, but so long as we remain married to our present financial system we will continue to have these problems arise, we will continue to be forced into debt, not only as the government of Canada but we will also drive other public groups into debt, notably the provinces and, what is even more serious, the municipalities.
The opinion of the C.C.F. has been expressed a great number of times in this house and elsewhere in the country about the necessity of maintaining control of our own financial structure in our own hands instead of leaving it in the hands of outside interests who from time to time can do nothing more than assist us to drive ourselves deeper into debt and to raise interest rates for ourselves and the provinces and the municipalities, not to mention the interest rates which individual citizens have to pay when they borrow money for various purposes. There is an old saying which is applicable in this case, by a person who said he did not care who controlled and who made the laws of a nation so long as he controlled and was able to issue the currency, and that is precisely the dilemma in which we are at the present time.
The provincial statistics show over the years a drastic and steady annual increase in the debt of those provinces because they could do nothing else under the circumstances but go into debt in order to finance their various projects. Worse still, there has been a drastic and steady increase in the total debt of the municipalities generally and in the debt of individual municipalities. Not only has there been an increase in the actual total amount of debt; there has also been an increase in the per capita debt and in the interest rates paid, all because our federal government is unable or unwilling to deal in a sensible fashion with the control of the finances of this country.
I have nothing more to say at this time. One could, as I have said, reiterate what we in the C.C.F. have said on many occasions previously in this session, and point out the effect that this conversion loan program will have on the municipalities and on bond rates and what it is doing in so far as tight or loose money is concerned. But that would be merely repetition and probably would not serve too useful a purpose at this time and, so long as this government is in office, it would not

serve too useful a purpose at any time in convincing the government that it is following the wrong road when it comes to the control of our own finances and our financial destiny.

Mr. Chairman, I want to say a few words on this bond conversion program. I was surprised when I heard that the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance had gone on the air as bond salesmen, and I really wondered what had come over them. I noted at the time that the early radio, television and press comments on this conversion really hailed the program, and I thought perhaps I had been taught the wrong concepts of mathematics.
I realized that due to the slackening economy our short term interest rate was approaching an all-time low. In fact, about the middle of last month it did reach an all-time low when the Canadian bank rate stood at 1.12 per cent and treasury bills at .87 per cent. I could not get out of my mind, either, that the average interest on the unmatured bond debt or the total debt of Canada stood at something under 3 per cent-2.98 per cent to be exact as of last March-and that when you took into consideration that the new long term 4J per cent bonds would bear interest at something over 1J per cent above our average, you could not help but feel that we in Canada would be spending many additional millions of dollars in taxes to meet this interest alone.
Every old bond issue was eligible for conversion into the long term 4J per cent bond issue on which the commission was the highest, namely 1 per cent. Certainly this was an inducement to channel all possible outstanding bonds into the high interest long term bonds, and the advertising emphasized that the long term, high interest bonds were most desirable. As we look at the advertising even on the application form for a bond we see that the printing respecting the 4J per cent long term bonds is in the larger type and the printing with respect to the other bonds is in progressively smaller type.
There was a statement that there were too many maturing bonds overhanging the market and that there was a need for tidying up the bond market. It is true that the fifth victory bond issue would come due next January and, as we have an election every four years, the eighth bond loan would not come due until after the next election and the ninth victory loan was not likely to come due until the election after that. In my mind it would seem that the minister certainly wanted no overhang. In fact, he trimmed it back so far that by no stretch of the imagination would any of these maturities bother him in the future.
Supply-Finance
I witnessed two transactions made in a bank, one for $10,000 of the fifth victory loan issue and the other for $5,000 of the eighth victory loan issue. The bank converted both these victory loan bonds into the 4J per cent long term bonds, and the bank's commission was $150. The client holding the $10,000 3 per cent victory loan bonds got new 4J per cent bonds plus $250, $51 of which was accrued interest and $199 of which was a bonus free of income tax. The cost to the Canadian taxpayers, therefore, to change this one $10,000 bond to the new 4J per cent bond was $350 which, of course, includes the $100 commission plus $250 bonus, including of course the accrued interest of $51. This, of course, does not include the proper apportionment of radio, television and advertising costs to convince this man to change his bonds.
This bank clerk had heard the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance make a great patriotic appeal to these victory bond holders to change their bonds to the 4| per cent bonds. I think we should all help our country, and I could not help but be impressed with the upsurge of patriotism that must have been in this man's heart as he took $250 as a bonus plus a new bond with the realization that, thanks to the Minister of Finance, henceforth he would get $450 instead of $300 for the use of this part of his money.
I told a financial man that I thought some of these commissions were too high, and he admitted it. We were talking about the 1 per cent and the 4J per cent bonds and he said, to quote his words, "It is a hell of a steal".

Mr. Chairman, if no other hon. members wish to address the committee on the Canada conversion loan of 1958, I shall now have very much pleasure in replying to some of the biting criticisms which have been heard in this committee today from the opposition benches with respect to this important national undertaking.
This morning the Leader of the Opposition complimented himself on, as he said, having acted responsibly in the days which have intervened since July 14 when the campaign was announced in this house until today. Mr. Chairman, having recognized that the Leader of the Opposition acted responsibly in his remarks in this house on July 14 and since by his silence, until today, one can only express great regret that today the hon. gentleman has chosen the opposite course. While one is ready to attribute to the hon. gentleman full credit for having spoken as he did on July 14 in a spontaneous utterance, one can only regret that apparently in the interval, and very recently, he has been permitting himself to be influenced by others.
I shall have something to say later, Mr. Chairman, about the compound of confusion

and suspicion that characterized some of the utterances in this committee today. 1 say this to you. Although the estimates of the Department of Finance have been called several times or announced several times as about to be called at other stages of the session, in the light of the remarks that have been made here today, which if they are listened to or paid any attention to by the people of this country, could have harmful effects perhaps, it is well that the Canada conversion loan campaign was permitted to reach the present stage in its second last week before those harmful remarks, those mischievous remarks, those irresponsible remarks, were delivered in this house by hon. gentlemen opposite.
Let me review stage by stage the circumstances out of which the Canada conversion loan campaign issued. We as a government inherited from our predecessors the prospect of the maturity in rapid succession of a considerable series of bond obligations of this country. They are not confined to the Canada victory loans; but of the $10 billion in approximate figures that the people of Canada subscribed in response to appeals during the war in the nine victory loan issues, up to the present time four have matured and have been refunded or in part paid off. Five of them remain, and those five aggregate something over $6.4 billion, a tremendous share of the entire national debt.
As I pointed out in the statement made in this house on July 14, the difficulty is that these five series are falling due in rapid succession. One of them falls due at the beginning of 1959.

There is nothing that is more important to the wellbeing of the Canadian economy in all its aspects, in all its facets, than the national credit, of this country; for if that national credit is not maintained and safeguarded the credit of other institutions and individuals will correspondingly suffer, Mr. Chairman; for the national credit is basic to all our ideas of credit and all ideas of confidence in our country.

Now, Mr. Chairman, there is with respect to a rapid succession of maturities virtually no room for manoeuvre on the part of the issuing authority. These are obligations which must be met as they fall due; otherwise serious and sometimes irreparable harm is done to the credit of the issuing authority. It is possible in some cases to anticipate a maturity and make an offer to those who hold bonds that will mature in the future to surrender them in return for some other form of security, normally under present circumstances in terms of a later maturity. I should like to say a word now concerning the condition of the bond market. The government is a debtor. The government must continue to be a borrower. One C.C.F. member said today that as long as we are going to have the present system you are going to have situations of this kind where the government has to offer obligations to people in return for maturing obligations, or borrow further money from them. He was right. As long as we have a free system in this country that is exactly the situation that any government is going to face. It must go into the market and borrow money there. It cannot go into the market and compel people to hand over money. It can do that when it taxes, but not when it borrows. Borrowing assumes that you find someone with funds who is willing to lend his funds to you, and the government as a borrower must find persons who are willing to lend money.

Anybody who knows anything of conditions in the market knows perfectly well that if these five issues of Canadian victory bonds had been permitted to remain outstanding until maturity without any effort being made to reduce the outstanding aggregate the

I stressed in my budget speech, Mr. Chairman, that there must be a relatively flexible approach to this problem on the part of the federal government. At page 1242 of Hansard for June 17, 1958, in the budget speech, this is what I said:
Government policy regarding the management of the public debt cannot follow any rigid formula; it must be adapted to economic conditions and to market requirements. While I do not propose to place an undue burden on the longer term bond market, it is most desirable to keep our maturing debt reasonably spread out over the years. To refinance maturing issues cheaply in the short term market would only build up greater difficulties for ourselves two or three years hence. It will be our aim to offer acceptable volumes of longer term bonds whenever suitable opportunities

occur, and to spread the remainder sensibly between short and mid-term maturities.
While the prospective increase in our debt will be quite substantial during the next year or two, the net burden of the public debt will remain well below what we carried quite easily only a few years ago.
I indicated there, Mr. Chairman, the necessity of preserving a measure of flexibility in our approach to this problem, and not being tied down to any rigid formula. What we have done since has been completely in keeping with that principle.
Now, it was a change in the market condition which was occurring at that time which necessarily had a very direct influence on our thinking and our approach to the problem of borrowing. Beginning on June 16, the day before the budget speech, there set in in the financial markets of the United States a rapid weakening which affected the strength of the bond market immediately, and that communicated itself to Canada as any weakness in the market in the United States does communicate itself to Canada. We had to take account therefore, of this weakening influence in the financial markets in the United States, a situation where yields were rising and the quoted values of securities of even the highest authority, the federal government, were dropping rapidly.
What happened in the United States in the middle of June continued, and has continued since. This situation was described in one of the leading financial periodicals in the United States, the regular letter of the Bankers' Trust Company, in these words:
The financial community has just witnessed a most unusual occurrence: the government bond market has undergone a precipitate drop-
Note these words, Mr. Chairman:
-a precipitate drop at a time when business activity is near its recession low following the sharpest decline since prewar days, and when the federal reserve has been furnishing reserves to the money market in massive amounts.
That is a United States estimate of the weakening that set in in the financial market there, and which had an immediate effect upon the values of government bonds in that country. We felt the result of that weakening and so, taking cognizance of the situation, we decided at that time to postpone any attempt to go to the financial markets of this country to borrow money on a new issue. In order to meet the temporary situation, as I fully explained to the house in my statement on July 14, we arranged temporary financing through the banks and the temporary financing is to continue until December.
In the meantime, Mr. Chairman, we undertook a measure by which we sought to bring, and I have no doubt have succeeded in bringing, abiding strength to the bond market in 57071-3-290;

Canada, and for the purpose and with the result of strengthening the position of the federal government and other governments in that market. This is our concern, that for whatever causes the federal government may have to go to the market for borrowings, we shall go there on as favourable terms as we can obtain. No minister of finance of this country is ever going to go to the bond market on terms that are any more generous than he has to pay to borrow the money he requires.
Faced with this situation, we turned to the Canada conversion loan as the largest financial undertaking in Canadian history, and designed to bring strength to the whole structure of borrowings in this country.
I do not need to go over the ground I have covered in previous statements in the house. This measure offers us an opportunity to bring about some control over our debt maturities that could not have been accomplished in any other way. The Leader of the Opposition talked glibly this morning about debt management, yet he condemned the one effective way by which debt management policies may be put into effect in this country. What is the use of talking like that? It is action that is required, and this conversion loan will do more to make it possible for the government to have some control over debt maturities and put into effect policies of effective debt management than anything else that could have been done under the circumstances.
I have indicated, Mr. Chairman, how these rates are set. The Minister of Finance, in going into the market, goes there to make his borrowings on the most favourable terms he can obtain. Those from whom the money is to be borrowed naturally are looking for the best rate they can obtain, and it becomes a matter then of arriving, in accordance with the estimate of supply and demand in as fine a scale as human judgment will permit, at those terms which will attract the money that is required to be borrowed on behalf of Canada. That is the way it will always be as long as we have a free economy in Canada.
Of course, if we are asking people in this country, to lend money to us for a longer period, anybody who knows anything about the bond market in recent years knows that we must be prepared to offer inducements, for the longer term market in these recent times has been more elusive by far than has the short term market and the yield rates in the long term market have been substantially higher than those in the short term market.

Our effort in this campaign, and one reason we have sought to make use of the various media of publicity, is to bring home to every holder of these bonds, even to the man who holds a $50 bond, the advantages that will accrue to him through this conversion and to see that he has the same opportunity of knowing about these advantages and making up his mind in the face of them as any holder of larger amounts of victory bonds.

The hon. gentleman asked first of all about the cost of publicity and he said his figure was $2 million. The actual budget for publicity is $1,500,000. That is one fortieth of 1 per cent of the total amount we are seeking to convert. Let me say this. If we had let these five issues of victory bonds ride along to maturity we would then have had to face the problem of publicity costs for five new loans to provide the money to meet these maturities on a refunding or other basis. Here we are getting five campaigns rolled into one with all the savings that come in publicity in rolling those five into one.
In the second place I stress the fact that we conceive it to be our duty to carry this information to the man who is a small holder of bonds, the man who may not be very experienced in dealing with bonds and who may hold a bond valued at $50, $100 or $500. If we had not undertaken this publicity campaign we would have been accused by hon. members opposite of being

Supply-Finance
interested only in seeking conversions by the large holders of these victory bonds.
The next question dealt with the dealers' commissions. I was told that we had not given adequate information to the house on various aspects of this Canada conversion loan. Mr. Chairman, I put all the information about the commissions on record in this house in reply to questions asked by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River and that information is to be found in Hansard of July 30. There I pointed out that the commission paid is graduated according to the maturity. Naturally, when we are urging people to convert their bonds into the most distant maturity the harder selling is there and we wanted to create as much incentive as we could in that quarter. The rates of commission that have been set are entirely reasonable and realistic. They were one quarter of 1 per cent on the 3 per cent bonds, one half of 1 per cent on the 3J per cent bonds, three quarters of 1 per cent on the 4J per cent bonds and 1 per cent on the 4J per cent bonds.
Then, Mr. Chairman, I was quick to add that we took out of the total the large amounts that would have been easier to be had by those who are doing the canvassing. What we did was to allow no commission whatever on conversions by the Bank of Canada. There is nothing to pay, of course, on conversions out of government accounts.

They get the one quarter of 1 per cent on the 3 per cent bonds but they get only one half of 1 per cent on the other three maturities. In that way we have taken steps to hold down the commissions and prevent easy commissions on the conversions of the larger holdings. That is all on record at page 2858 of Hansard of July 30, 1958. I pointed out there that the commission to this group is one quarter of 1 per cent on the 3 per cent bonds and one half of 1 per cent on all other maturities.
I was asked to compare these rates of commission with those on the Canada savings bonds campaigns of 1955, 1956 and 1957. The commission paid in each of those savings bonds issues was three quarters of 1 per cent and the issuing and redemption fee in all cases was one quarter of 1 per cent. I said then and I repeat now it is quite clear that

The next question was this: "Who held those bonds?" That is, held the bonds, let us say, on July 11, which was the last day of business, the Friday prior to the inauguration of this campaign on Monday, July 14. Mr. Chairman, some of his figures on this were not inaccurate. The Bank of Canada held approximately $1J billion; government accounts held approximately $435 million; chartered banks approximately $1.4 billion; and then the large institutions that we heard so much about today held about $1.2 billion; and then there are the other investors. These are your people in the rank and file of Canadians, these are your people who include small investors, very small businesses, everybody outside the class of large institutions, and when I say "outside the class of large institutions" in referring to that exempt names list, there were 1,200 included in it.

Therefore, you see that all of the mediumsized as well as large institutions were included therein and not in the class of other investors. The figure of holdings on July 11 of those other investors, the small people in Canada, was, in round figures, $2.1 billion. Against that the Leader of the Opposition in this house today undertakes to quote as if it were fact the statement of a professor of Carleton University who said very truthfully that he did not know how much was held by the small investors in Canada. Never did the gentleman utter a truer statement than that.
But he went on from that point, having departed from a factual statement, to embark on an adventure into fancy and he said it might be 10 per cent or 15 per cent. Mr. Chairman, those figures show that not less than one-third of all of the outstanding victory bonds were held by people who can be described properly, in the ordinary sense of the word, as the small investors of Canada. How many of them were there? We have had today the most extraordinary statements made in this house by hon. members opposite about how few Canadians really hold those victory bonds. Mr. Chairman, no one can calculate exactly how many persons hold those outstanding victory bonds. Many of them are in bearer form. Large numbers of them are held by banks in safekeeping for their depositors, and in that case the figures which are shown here are the figures of the bank.
Now, a lot of the money that has been subscribed by the banks in the course of conversion has undoubtedly been the money of small depositors who leave their small victory bonds with the banks but no one knows the exact number. However, by long experience, those who have responsibility in the Bank of Canada and in the Department of Finance are able to make a rather shrewd estimate of the number of holders from the number and amounts of the certificates outstanding. Particularly is this the case in the small certificates. And here, Mr. Chairman, is the substance of statements issued by the Bank of Canada on August 12, that on the last count just before the Canada conversion loan was announced there were about 1,898,000, $100 pieces and 857,000, $50 pieces outstanding. It is on evidence like that that the estimate has been arrived at, that there were in this class of small investors in Canada holding one-third of the outstanding victory bonds approximately 2 million persons. That is, sir, the answer to hon. members opposite who talk about this conversion loan playing into the hands of big business. These shocking, irresponsible and reprehensible statements which

Supply-Finance
were made here today about windfalls will remain on the record as a test of the responsibility of certain hon. members opposite.
Then, Mr. Chairman, what about insurance companies? Some of the large holdings were in the hands of insurance companies. The insurance companies acquire the bonds or convert them for the benefit of their hundreds of thousands of policyholders. And what about the trusts which are set up, the university endowments and all manner of trusts of that kind? These are trusts in most cases for persons of limited means, but in these figures they are bulked in together and railed at by hon. members opposite as the holdings of big business. If ever this house has seen misrepresentation of the facts, utter distortion of the facts, Mr. Chairman, it has seen it in the house today.
The next question I was asked by the Leader of the Opposition was, what will be the effect on interest rates, first, on the long term and short term maturities and then on the securities of provinces and municipalities? I cannot prophesy, Mr. Chairman, the course of interest rates over the next few years or, indeed, over the next period of months, but I will say, without fear of contradiction on the part of any responsible source in this country that the effect of the Canada conversion loan has been to stabilize the market and in that way it has contributed not only to preventing a further rise in interest rates but in checking it and turning the tide in that respect. That is the effect of this issue.

The Leader of the Opposition's eleventh question was, why did you not announce this program in the budget speech? The simple answer is that we had not at that time undertaken the planning of the Canada conversion loan. We were aware of this large problem of the five victory loan issues aggregating $6.4 billion overhanging the market, acting as a weight on the market, and to that extent hampering the efforts of everyone in borrowing. We were aware of the problem and I referred in my budget speech at that time to the necessity for a flexible approach. It was in terms of a flexible approach that, with the change in conditions which set in the day before the budget speech and moved along rapidly in the days that followed, we undertook this constructive campaign.
His twelfth question was, why did you include the eighth and ninth victory loans in the general conversion offering? There are several reasons. Those who responded in time of war to Canada's necessity and subscribed to victory loan bonds were not divided into rigid categories. They were all persons who responded in that way. I do not think it would have gone very well if we had sought to discriminate now in the Canada conversion 57071-3-2914
Supply-Finance
loan offering among the holders of different maturities of victory loan issues. In the second place, if we had to go to this tremendous effort and incur this expense in the course of promoting the campaign, does it not make good sense to include the five in the one operation rather than include only three in the one operation and still leave outstanding, to be faced when they fell due in 1963 and 1966, approximately another $24 billion of maturing victory loan bonds of the eighth and ninth series? These are broadly the reasons.
There is another that I think might be mentioned and that is that these latter series of victory loan bonds have a callable feature. They are callable five years before maturity and from the point of view of the investor that uncertainty has a very unsettling effect. To the extent that this eighth and ninth series represent about $2.5 billion overhanging the market, with all the uncertainty attached to them and the depressing effect that has on values, surely it was good sense and good business to take in now all the outstanding series of victory loans.
I regret, Mr. Chairman, having detained the committee so long. I regret it sincerely. I regret the occasion. I was asked today why I did not reply on an earlier occasion to some of the statements made by members of the C.C.F. when they spoke in this house on August 5 and 6. To be quite frank, I can say to you that at that time I felt that statements of the kind that were made by them on those two days deserved only to be ignored, so far were they from the fact and from simple, decent, Canadian justice as between man and man. It would have suited me very well if it had not been necessary to say anything at all or to answer questions on this matter. It became necessary to deal with these matters fully in reply to the attacks that have been heard in this house today.
Mr. Chairman, let me conclude my remarks. We have had, I submit, such a response from the Canadian people as demonstrates, not only their confidence in Canada but their confidence in Canada as an object for their lending. This kind of confidence, this kind of response, is not confined simply to the kind of people who were the object of some rather haranguing statements made in this house today. Let me tell hon. members that the provinces and municipalities in this country were, themselves, substantial holders of Canada victory bonds, and their response has been what one would expect. Here is Newfoundland with various accounts, the Newfoundland savings bank, the Newfoundland workmen's compensation board, who held something over $3 million of these bonds. Up to August 25, they had converted 90 per

Coming back to the remarks of the hon. member for Welland, if one can apprehend what he was driving at, I should like to add this on the point. In accepting the terms and conditions of the Canada conversion loan all primary distributors agreed to arrange conversions with clients only on the basis outlined in the official prospectus. This kind of arrangement is a normal feature of any offering of new securities.
Dealers found there were some holders of victory bonds who preferred to sell their bonds rather than convert them and other investors who did not own victory bonds but wanted to buy new conversion bonds for cash. Sales and purchases of victory bonds did not always match off for each dealer each day and price fluctuations occurred which made it sometimes possible for investors to sell victory bonds for cash and buy conversion bonds for cash on more favourable terms than by a straight conversion. Such a situation was increasingly causing delays in conversion as some investors held
Supply-Finance
off to see if they could obtain better terms, and it involved discrimination.
On August 7, on the strong recommendation of the national committee formed to promote the conversion loan, fixed prices were stipulated at which distributors might buy victory bonds from customers and sell conversion bonds for cash to customers. The effect of these prices was to put matched cash transactions and straight conversions on the same basis so far as dealer remuneration and investor cost are concerned. I am assured that the effect of this action has been the elimination of discriminatory treatment and a larger total response to the government's conversion offer.
Mr. Chairman, I was asked today by the Leader of the Opposition what the policy of the government is in relation to monetary questions. So far as questions of monetary policy enter into the Canada conversion loan and they do enter into it-let me make it abundantly clear that the policy of this government, as clearly enunciated by the Prime Minister in the broadcast on the night of July 14, is a policy of sound money.
What this government has said it intends to do, and to do in relation to this offering to the Canadian people, is to take such steps as are within the power of the government to maintain the stability and the purchasing power of the Canadian dollar and this campaign is to bring about a situation with reference to this large section of the public debt of Canada where we have some control over maturities, where we can apply policy of debt management. This Canada conversion loan fits into that policy and is going to strengthen our hands in carrying out that beneficent policy for the benefit of Canadians in the years to come.
Mr. Chairman, there has been criticism. I do not mind the personal criticism that has been directed at me. I will close my remarks today with this prophecy. Succeeding ministers of finance whether they be Liberal or whether they be Conservative will have reason to be thankful in these days ahead that the government of 1958 had the vision and the courage and the realism to undertake this, the greatest financial operation in Canada's history.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF STRIKE
speechtext: The minister will need all the energy he has at his command. I am sorry he has found it necessary to use so much in his first performance on his estimates. During that time, as is customary over the years in this house, he indulged in a good deal of verbal ferocity and included in his remarks a good many jibes, one or two of them extremely cheap ones. As is his custom also, he mistakes, as he has done so often in the past, acid assertions for argument and vehemence for veracity. At this stage in our proceedings, Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to correct-though perhaps as we go through his estimates there will be the chance to correct some of them-the misstatements that he has made this afternoon. He accused us on this side of the house of irresponsibility in the intervention that was made by us of this subject this morning. He accused us of irresponsibility in bringing this matter to the attention of the committee in the way in which we did. But during the weeks since the announcement was made in this house that there was to be this operation of a magnitude and importance never before seen in our country he has given us no information of any kind concerning it; nothing at all. Nothing at all!

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF STRIKE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-INQUIRY AS TO STATUS OF STRIKE
speechtext:
He has given no information to this house at all concerning this matter and when my hon. friends of the C.C.F. raised the matter in debate he said nothing about it. He has explained this afternoon that the reason why he said nothing about it was that

their arguments were hardly worth-while replying to. He did say something, he intervened with such remarks as "Rubbish" and "Nonsense", but that is the contribution we have had from the Minister of Finance since July 14 until September 4 on this very important matter.
Today, however, he got up for two hours, or nearly two hours, and indulged in the kind of diatribe to which we have listened. What were we to do when his estimates came up? What were we to do during all these weeks- say everything is fine, the loan is going along, it is a wonderful operation and there is nothing in it to criticize? We were to say that we have complete confidence in the government and were to get finished and go home as soon as we got the minister's estimates through. That is what he would have liked us to do, but that is not our responsibility to the nation and that is not how we are going to discharge what we consider to be our responsibility to the nation.
The minister said that on July 14, when the announcement was first made about this loan, when I got up in the house after the announcement I adopted a position of high responsibility but now in speaking for my party that I have descended from what he considered to be those heights of responsibility.
I would remind the minister that when he made that announcement in the house it was without any prior information having been given to the leader of any other party. He did not take anybody into his confidence, even one hour before the announcement was made. He simply got up in this house and made the announcement and even at that time he did not tell the whole story. I am not complaining about that because it could not be done on motions. However, I said at that time-and the same stand was taken by the leader of the C.C.F.-realizing that this was an operation of the magnitude and importance which we now know it to be, that it was important in the national interest as it is today important in the national interest, that this operation should not fail.
In making that statement I said that I would follow this operation with interest. We have been following it with interest, we have been studying it, and as a result of the information we have acquired and of the studies we have made we have put forward our attitude in this regard in the words I used this morning-we have done it less than ten days before the end of the operation- when it has reached its last stages. It was better the debate should be done now, in view of the fact that if it had taken place four or five weeks ago perhaps there might

have been misunderstandings and misleading impressions created by the criticism we were bound as an opposition to make to the way in which this operation was being conducted -not of the objective of the conversion, but to the methods.
If the minister had been fair he would have said when he got up to reply that twice when I spoke today I stated that we approved of the objective of the conversion. We believe that this effort should be successful, but we do not approve of some of the details and some of the ways in which it was being carried out. If that is irresponsibility I would remind the minister of some of the things he said in this house when he talked about financial matters in other days. I suggest to the minister that we have shown him a great deal more consideration in this matter than he ever showed his predecessor, the former minister of finance, when he talked about financial matters.

country with respect to the conversion loan? Why did he wait until September 4 to put these figures on record if he was trying to put this loan across, as he said, because it must be put across as it is a great national effort, and so on? Why did he allow these misleading reports to be circulated in the country? Why did he wait until the last day of the session when he was baited into it by the questions we asked?
In another part of his statement he put on record a lot of figures to show that the municipalities, who are going to pay more for their money, have converted their bonds into the new loan and because some of those municipalities are headed by two members on this side of the house, he paid them a special tribute as being loyal and patriotic Canadians. I ask, why should not any municipality take advantage of this windfall loan, which is the expression used by those who are trying to sell it?
What particular significance is there to be attached to that as a vindication of the policy of the government? The policy of the government in this matter will be determined by the results of this loan after it is finished and the effect it has on the money market and our economic prospects. We on this side are willing to let it stand on that basis. But to think that the Minister of Finance who used to talk so much on this side on every financial occasion and used his undoubted ability to marshal adjectives if not arguments to pillory the government should expect us to sit quiet and say nothing about this operation-because if we ask questions and make criticisms we are then considered irresponsible-is almost beyond belief. The test of irresponsibility in this matter will be the results of the government's operation. That will be a better test than anything that could be said on this side of the house and we are quite willing to let it rest on that basis.

I would prefer to put it on the basis of the yields.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to get the minister going again because whenever he gets going we are exposed to a two-hour speech and he behaves like an offended virgin every time he is criticized. However, I do want to ask him a question or two.
I believe I indicated earlier that the last time we as a federal entity had been obliged to pay 4J per cent interest it was again wages for money such as was introduced by a Conservative administration but even then-and I think it was 1934-they had a 10-year provision for a callable privilege. Succeeding Liberal governments with more prudent administration found circumstances under which they were able to pay off that high rate of bond indebtedness. I referred this morning to how old the minister would be 25 years from now. I cannot understand why he would commit the future taxpayers of Canada in the next generation to an unavoidable 4J per cent obligation on debt which I think is not synonymous with thoughtful behaviour. A businessman hesitates twice when thinking in terms of a rate that goes much beyond 5| or 6 per cent when he is asked to pay 6, 7 or 8 per cent for any investment he has in mind, an investment that might create unemployment at the present time. I just cannot understand the undeviating base that is being put on interest rates in this country for another 25 years because of the non-callable feature.

That means that the government has now increased the interest paid to citizens of Canada, banks and other institutions by $5.66 per person per annum because the government will now be paying $289,125,000 in interest per year. All I can say is that I am suspicious of long defences. I am astonished at the minister's long defence and the old French proverb, qui s'excuse s'accuse, applies to him perfectly.
The minister takes pride in the fact that 80 or 85 per cent of the sale has been completed. Of course; it is such a bargain, who would not want to buy? Surely the minister realizes, as I do, that if he wanted to sell more and do so faster all he had to do was to fix a five per cent return or perhaps a six per cent return and he would have had results very much faster. But this is my criticism, and this is what members of the opposition have said. The country has been called upon to make this financial effort. Why? I think the government found itself in difficulty. It has to meet its election promises, it has to meet a great deficit and it has launched into this great expense which I think the country will remember for a great many years to come.

I will be very glad to deal with that subject. I think the Leader of the Opposition has probably overlooked the fact that, as I recall it, there was some discussion of it on the estimates of my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, but I am happy to deal with it. The conference will open in Montreal on Monday, September 15. It is expected to continue until Friday, September 26. It will thus run, it is expected, for two weeks. All of the commonwealth countries will be represented at the conference by ministers and delegations and the delegation from the United Kingdom, which will consist of five ministers and a number of advisers, will be accompanied also in an advisory capacity by six ministers drawn from various colonies in different parts of the world.
The agenda which the conference is likely to take up will be a very broad one. Trade is one subject, but trade is only one aspect. The agenda is expected to embrace broadly all questions pertaining to the economic relations of the various nations of the commonwealth. The meeting is to proceed in the Queen Elizabeth hotel. The secretary-general of the conference, by agreement of the commonwealth countries, is to be Mr. Sydney Pierce who, as hon. members will recall, has been latterly the deputy high commissioner of this country in the United Kingdom. A good deal of work has been expended by officials in preparation for this conference. The departments of government principally concerned are, of course, finance, trade and commerce and external affairs.
The conference is preceded by several conferences of officials of the commonwealth countries at various stages of preparation during the recent months. I shall be glad to answer any further questions if there are any.

After all, this is a conference on commonwealth economic relationships, to be presided over by the minister. It is a conference which has been put forward by the government as one of the most important to be held within the commonwealth, and one which will have far-reaching results on the economic, financial, and therefore on the political relationships of members inside the commonwealth. I think it is unfortunate that we have not had the kind of discussion about this conference, as important as it is, that has been had in the parliament at Westminster. I think it is unfortunate that even, at this late date we can only be told in general terms what will be the nature of the subjects dealt with and the policy of the Canadian government in respect of these matters.
There is an impression which one gets from the press that, whereas a year ago this conference was being heralded as one of very great importance, primarily in respect of trade relationships between members of the commonwealth-we heard a great deal at that time about the diversion of trade that
might result from a conference of that kind_
latterly, that impression of a year ago seems to have disappeared and there seems to be a contrary impression, at least in the minds of the press, that perhaps the most important subject for discussion will be the financial relationships between the members and India and what certain members of the commonwealth can do in respect of strengthening what is now called international liquidity.
We all know that when the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom came to Washington, and Ottawa a few months ago, he announced.

In press statements in both Ottawa and Washington that it was of vital importance to do something to put the underdeveloped countries of the world in possession of hard currency, thereby giving them a chance to develop. This suggestion has been taken up by other governments, notably by our own Prime Minister who made an announcement about it subsequently in this House of Commons as well as statements about it outside of the house. This seems to be one of the subjects which is going to loom up in the agenda of this conference. Of course, the minister knows that this is a subject which cannot be finally determined on a commonwealth basis. However, the preliminary discussions there might be quite useful, and perhaps more far-reaching results will be achieved at the meeting of the fund and the bank which will be held subsequent to the meeting.
As a matter of fact, as the minister knows, it has become the custom to have a meeting of commonwealth finance ministers before the meeting of the bank.

I have been to a lot of conferences and I know it is quite unwise, but perhaps quite natural, to exaggerate the importance of everything about the conference, prior to the opening of it; but you begin to realize that all the things you put forward in your own interests, the things that are going to be accomplished by your policies are not likely to result and therefore an element of caution is being introduced even at this late date. Perhaps that is realistic and sensible. We know very little in this house what the policy of the government is in respect of these matters. Then, it goes on to discuss in a very general way British

The others items on the agenda will be the special and urgent help needed by India-
That is something that will be of interest to the Canadian government.
- (and it is probable that the terms of the new British loan may not be announced until the conference) : measures to stabilize commodity prices; the direction of economic expansion in the less developed countries, with new ways of providing capital and helping trade; technical assistance for these countries; economic and trading difficulties connected with agricultural and other primary production; the prospects and implications of the European common market and the proposed European free trade area; and arrangements for continuing commonwealth consultations and co-operation on economic matters.
This is a much more detailed agenda than we have received in this committee or than was given out after the meeting at Mont Tremblant last year. I, therefore, express some disappointment that we have not had the kind of discussion before a conference of this importance which I think perhaps we should have had. I know the minister could not fail to agree with me on this because he used to talk a good deal about the failure to have discussion in parliament before we, in our day, went to international conferences. The minister had this to say, and I commend it to him as the policy that might now be followed:
If parliamentary institutions enjoyed here in Ottawa the health that they ought to enjoy, no Canadian prime minister-
Or indeed no minister of finance, if I may interpolate that remark.
-would go to an important commonwealth conference without having first invited a discussion in parliament on the position that he was going to take on behalf of his country in the deliberations of that conference. But such is the treatment that this government metes out to our Canadian parliament, such is the conspiracy of silence of this government on important national issues, such apparently is the minimum importance that this government attaches to this commonwealth prime ministers' conference, there is not to be a word said in this house even on the subject of the agenda. A fine demonstration of contempt for the parliament of Canada!
Then he goes on to say this:
We might at least have had a debate on the subject, but apparently we are not going to have, even during the course of this discursive debate on
