I thank the Leader of the Opposition for his closing words. The government will appreciate them very much. I think I should remind the Leader of the Opposition, in view of the fact that he spoke about debate, that I dealt with this subject in the budget speech, as will be found at page 1239 of Hansard of June 17. I reviewed the position and indicated the broad lines that we would be following at the conference in the matter of trade policy. It is all set out there very clearly.
The hon. gentleman also raised the question about emphasis at the conference. This from the beginning was always announced and regarded as a commonwealth trade and economic conference. At no time was there any suggestion that the conference should be confined to trade matters. Indeed, the economic matters on which, as a result of study, we find that commonwealth countries have common or mutual interests have been expanding and all of them are of high importance. Under developing conditions some of them are assuming more and more importance. I do not need to dwell here on questions of development of resources and the strains that have been created by programs of that kind and problems of exchange scarcities on the economic relations of countries of the commonwealth. I stressed in the budget speech that the commonwealth today is a very different commonwealth from that of 1932. Our approach to the problems that will confront us at the conference is very different from that of 1932.
My hon. friend spoke about the problem of liquidity. This is a very acute problem. It touches a good many of the economic factors in the situation and it touches on trade as well. I think it lies at the basis of a good many of the media that are used today which have the effect of restraining a trade, the whole problem of exchange restrictions and discrimination. These are associated and have

been associated over the years, in the case of a number of commonwealth countries, with the exchange problem, the problem of exchange reserves. These problems must all be examined at this conference. Indeed, Mr. Chairman, there is such a multiplicity of problems of an economic nature which cannot be categorized as trade matters that it is small wonder that in the public comment on this conference the emphasis has come increasingly to be laid on the economic problems that will be submitted to the conference for discussion.
As to the agenda, I thought I was elucidating the matter by stressing the fact that the agenda is really so broad that any question of an economic nature of interest to commonwealth countries can be discussed under it. The annual meetings of finance ministers in times past have related to the position of sterling in the world. It has been customary for the chancellor of the exchequer to make a report on that matter. Then in recent years there has naturally been a good deal of interest in the commonwealth countries, particularly those that are shipping food products to the United Kingdom, in Britain's relationship to the developing free trade area in Europe. I touched on that matter in the budget speech. The agenda is a matter of public record. It is in the communique that was issued at the Mont Tremblant conference. I stressed that the study that has been given to the agenda in the interval has all been within the framework of that laid down under the communique issued a year ago.

I wonder whether in these practical subjects, in these subsections of the agenda, special consideration will be given-and I am sure it will be because the minister rather indicated it-to matters which I think perhaps are of importance and that I know will be before the conference.
One is convertibility which he mentioned. Until we can make progress there we are going to have a hard time making progress in trade. As he knows, in recent years, progress has been made. However, it has been wavering progress and there have been difficulties

which impeded it. I would hope now, because conditions are improving in the world, that a real push can be given toward convertibility.
Then related to that matter-and the London Times mentions this as a step further and perhaps it is on the agenda-is the relationship of at least some commonwealth countries to the European free trade area and the common market. I do not know of anything that will be more important in the long run, and maybe not such a long run. An effort has to be made to work out our relationships to this European development. It is primarily perhaps a problem for the United Kingdom because they have been engaged in a search for a solution for some time. But it is almost as important for Canada because if the United Kingdom-and surely this will be discussed at this conference-does not make an arrangement with the European free trade area, we will all be in trouble outside of the United Kingdom and maybe even the United Kingdom itself. At the same time I should hate to see the United Kingdom use the commonwealth association as a reason for not making the kind of arrangement with the European free trade area which I think is essential not only for the development of Europe but for the development of what I consider to be a major body of international economic policy, namely an Atlantic freer trade area.

Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker, P.C., M.P.,
Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa.
In the Newfoundland legislature today I moved and Mr. Hollett the Leader of the Opposition seconded and the house unanimously adopted the following motion-
This is the text of the resolution:
Resolved the House of Assembly cordially welcomes the announcement of the Prime Minister, Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker made in the House of Commons on August 15, 1958, that the government of Canada would not accept the recommendations of the royal commission on term 29 until they have had opportunity to give the matter more careful study. The Prime Minister's announcement is all the more welcome to this house because of the reason he gave for it namely that there appeared to be dissatisfaction in Newfoundland with the size of the amount recommended. This house declares its warm appreciation of the Prime Minister's stand and expresses the hope that it will result in a substantial increase in the size of the amount ultimately to be paid to the province on a lasting basis. In the meanwhile we urgently request the government of Canada to seek without delay the necessary parliamentary authority to pay to Newfoundland in the present session as an interim measure at least the amount that has been recommended by the royal commission. This would enable the public services and public works of the province to be continued this year without interruption or reduction thereby preventing immediate widespread unemployment and would provide ample time before the next session of parliament for the Prime Minister and his colleagues in the government of Canada to give that further study announced by the Prime Minister.
The message was signed "J. R. Smallwood". I should like to repeat that this resolution was a bi-partisan resolution moved by the

premier and seconded by the leader of the opposition, something not very usual in any of our legislative assemblies or in our parliament except on the most formal occasions. There is also other evidence I could adduce but I do not intend to take up the time of the committee in doing so. This may be taken to represent the substantial unanimity that exists in the province of Newfoundland on this very pressing question.
Lest it be thought this is a very late hour at which the assembly of Newfoundland is raising this question I will say no more than that a formal request was made, as the minister well knows, to the Prime Minister by the premier of Newfoundland in the same general terms as early as August 11, so this is not a last minute request. It is simply further evidence of how extremely urgent this is to the people-not to the government but to the people-of Newfoundland that there should be action to implement the recommendations of the McNair report at this session of parliament.
As we all know that would not be a complicated or difficult matter. All the government would have to do is bring in a message from His Excellency with a further supplementary estimate to deal with this matter before the appropriation bill is before us.
Nowhere in any public statement I have seen or heard of in any part of Canada since the report was published on July 25 is it suggested that the award is too large. There is a great deal of dissatisfaction in Newfoundland which has been supported by criticisms in other places. For example, the Fredericton Gleaner, a newspaper not exactly noted for its support of our party but which has been pretty consistent in its support of hon. gentlemen opposite, has supported the contention of the leader of the house and the leader of the opposition and many others in Newfoundland that the award is inadequate.
But that is not the question I seek to put before the minister or the committee at the present time. I am not seeking to debate the merits of the recommendation nor am I attempting to divert attention from the point. Since it has been suggested nowhere that the award is too large and as it is needed, as I shall seek to show, for absolutely essential services in the province of Newfoundland, we at this session and before it prorogues should meet this solemn obligation of the constitution. I describe it in that language because that is what it is.
This is not a report of an ordinary royal commission as hon. members well know. This royal commission was set up pursuant to the terms of union with Newfoundland and pursuant particularly to term 29 of the terms of union. Even though it may take a little time

I feel I ought to refresh the memories of hon. members by putting the language of term 29 on the record because the whole of the subsequent argument, the whole case for urgent action, depends upon the legal and constitutional basis, the solemn obligation that our country entered into ten years ago, to carry out this term. Term 29 reads:
In view of the difficulty of predicting with sufficient accuracy the financial consequences to Newfoundland of becoming a province of Canada, the government of Canada will appoint a royal commission within eight years from the date of union to review the financial position of the province of Newfoundland and to recommend the form and scale of additional financial assistance, if any, that may be required by the government of the province of Newfoundland to enable it to continue public services at the levels and standards reached subsequent to the date of union, without resorting to taxation more burdensome, having regard to capacity to pay, than that obtaining generally in the region comprising the maritime provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Prince Edward Island.

Mr. Chairman, when we rose at six o'clock for the dinner recess I had just put on the record for the benefit of hon. members the text of term 29 of the terms of the union between Canada and Newfoundland, and as briefly as I can I want to point out just precisely what it is that the commissioners were asked to do and what it is that the government of Canada is obligated to do under this solemn undertaking given at the time of union.
The purpose of the commission was to review the financial position of the province of Newfoundland-and this is the important part-and to recommend the form and scale of additional financial assistance, if any, that may be required by the government of Newfoundland for two purposes, first, in order to continue public services at the levels and standards they had reached. Now, I want to emphasize that point to all hon. members. This award, this recommendation, of the McNair commission, is not designed or intended to improve the services in Newfoundland. All that it is intended to do is to continue them at the level they have now reached, or that they had reached at the time the commissioners were taking their evidence. Therefore, this is not something to raise standards in Newfoundland at all. This is simply something that will enable the government in that province to continue the standards attained and to do so without having a provincial tax structure more burdensome than the tax structure on the average of the three maritime provinces.
I want to emphasize the fact that there was no thought in this provision of the terms *of union that any award was to be made to bring the level of Newfoundland up to that of the highest province, or the Canadian average, or even up to the level of the other maritime provinces. All that it was to do under this particular provision was to continue the existing levels and standards of services, and to do that with a burden of taxation no heavier than that in the three maritime provinces. That is all the commission had the right or the power to award; but that is our solemn responsibility in this parliament to carry out one of the articles of the terms of union, to uphold one of the provincial rights of the government and the people of Newfoundland and I submit it is our duty to do so at the earliest possible date.
In order to save time although 1 would like very much to do it, I am not going to read what the commission said on this subject, though it is very brief. The commission found that the levels and standards of services

of the province of Newfoundland were still far below those of the rest of Canada and below those of the maritime provinces. That evidence will be found particularly at pages 8 and 9 of the report, but I repeat, the commission had no power to recommend that anything should be done to improve those levels and standards. All they could recommend was that there should be sufficient financial assistance to continue those levels and standards. The commission found-and this will be found at page 37 of the report, but I do not intend even to read it; I will just allude to it-that the burden of taxation in the province of Newfoundland was approximately equal to the average burden of taxation in the three maritime provinces. I admit this is a very difficult thing to measure and the commission said so; but I do not think there would be very great quarrel anywhere with the conclusion of the commission on that point. That means, of course, that any deficiency in revenue to maintain the existing levels and standards should not be made up by increasing provincial taxation in Newfoundland, since it was already as burdensome as in the maritime provinces, but should be made up by additional financial assistance to which the province, I emphasize, has a constitutional right under the terms of union, under the British North America Act. The commission found the deficiency to be $8 million per annum. That will be found- and it is very briefly stated-on page 40 of the report.
As I said at the beginning, and I repeat so that it will be here at this point, there is a good deal of dissatisfaction in Newfoundland, expressed by the premier, by the leader of the opposition, and by many others, that this recommendation is too low. The provincial commission recommended to the federal commission a sum almost twice as great, but I do not want to enter into that question now because it is one that the Prime Minister has promised us would be carefully considered by the government. I think we, too, like the premier of Newfoundland and the leader of the opposition, are very grateful for that undertaking on the part of the Prime Minister, as the unanimous resolution of the legislature says they are, and that question I think should be debated at another time.
What we are seeking to put forward now is to urge the government to meet this request, this bi-partisan request from Newfoundland, and to make as an interim payment the amount recommended by the commission.
There are those who may think that $8 million a year, in addition to what the province has, is a very large sum of money, but I might point out that under term 28 of the terms of union provision was made during

the first 12 years of union for transitional grants pending the determination of the permanent amount under term 29. For the first three years after confederation that transitional grant was $6,500,000, at a time when Newfoundland had roughly three-quarters of the population it has today. It may surprise some hon. members to realize how very rapid the increase in the population has been. Perhaps four-fifths would be a little more accurate than three-quarters. I have done my arithmetic rather rapidly. Those transitional grants were gradually to decrease until last year the amount was $1,400,000. This year it is $1,050,000, and it will be increasingly less next year.
I should like to point out to hon. members that last year, for various reasons which I am not going to enter into, the government of Newfoundland was not in a position to carry out many of the capital works which were planned for that year. That was not because of inclement weather or because the works did not need to be done, it was because finance was not available, and part of the reason why finance was not available was the steady decline in the amount of those transitional grants.
The award of the McNair commission is dated from April 1, 1957, which is, of course, the right date because that is the end of the eight-year period provided for in the constitution.
Therefore the amount that would be due at the present time is two years' instalment. It is provided in the report that the transitional grant should be deducted from the $8 million during the period of transitional grants so that the net amount that would be coming to the province this year and on which, since the report was published on July 25, the provincial authorities have been counting and have been expecting this parliament to make available to them, is approximately $13,500,000. I say again that this is a solemn obligation on the part of Canada, an obligation entered into at the time of union.
So much importance was attached to this solemn obligation that, as the hon. member for St. John's West will well recall, it was the policy of his party when he was in parliament some time ago to pledge themselves in advance at that time to carry out whatever the recommendations might be of the commission to be appointed, and there was some criticism of the Liberal government that the hon. gentleman will probably recall. I am not seeking to be controversial about this matter because I think the minister was showing a very commendable zeal for and interest in Newfoundland at that time, as he has since and as he did during the 1957 election campaign. I commend him for it. That
Supply-Finance
was one of the principal grounds on which he urged the electors to elect him, so that he would be here to see that Newfoundland did get a fair deal in this matter. I would not be surprised if the hon. gentleman had had something to do with influencing the Prime Minister to look over the matter again to see if there could not be a larger award made to Newfoundland. But nobody knows better than the minister how urgently necessary it is that this money should be paid if the works so badly needed in Newfoundland at the present time both to raise the standards of that province to a higher level and to provide employment are to be carried on.
I know it has been argued that because Newfoundland has received $7i million this year under the Atlantic provinces grants, as well as an additional payment similar to that made to all the other provinces because of the additional 3 per cent of the income tax, Newfoundland should have plenty of money to carry on this year. But let me remind hon. members what the situation is. The premier of the province, like the premiers of the other Atlantic provinces, had already announced his plans to use the Atlantic provinces grant in the same way that Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island can use them, not just to continue existing services but to improve services to bring them a little nearer to the level they have in Saskatchewan, and that is an entirely different thing. When the legislation covering the Atlantic provinces grants was introduced in the house we were told by the minister that their purpose was to raise levels in the Atlantic provinces.
What is going to happen this year has been explained very clearly in the budget speech delivered on Wednesday of last week, if I remember correctly, in the assembly at St. John's. The budget speech pointed out that if this payment under the McNair award was not made so that the province could use it for the purposes for which they are designed, to continue existing services, the Atlantic provinces grant in Newfoundland would have to be used to continue existing services and therefore could not be used for the purpose for which parliament intended it, namely to improve the situation in that province. Unless we act at this session we are going to be saying to Newfoundland, you have to use the Atlantic provinces grant to continue your existing services; you cannot use it the way the other Atlantic provinces can, to improve your services. And why? Because we in parliament are not carrying out our solemn undertaking, our constitutional obligation under the British North America Act. That is what we will be saying. I cannot believe that any member of this

S upp ly-Finance
parliament having considered the facts, because these are facts, would want to do that.
In view of conditions in Newfoundland, which have been particularly adverse this year because of the failure of the fishery and because of the difficulty of disposing of the pulp and paper products of the only other large Newfoundland industry, there is no question that the economic situation is very serious. Maintenance of existing services is going to be more difficult this year than it has been any year since confederation, particularly during the coming winter. Capital works are very urgently needed indeed. The school population of Newfoundland in proportion to the whole population is higher than it is in any other province of Canada. The shortage of schools is more acute there than anywhere else. The shortage of roads and the condition of the roads are such that there is a more urgent need for new and improved roads there than in any other part of Canada.
I could go on about all the services. No one needs to take my view of them because it is set out in the report of the royal commission. It is set out in the budget speech in Newfoundland the other day and it is a matter of common knowledge to all those who are familiar with the situation in that part of Canada. If the provincial government does not receive this money, which we have an obligation to pay to them and which they have the right to receive under the constitution, it means that the capital works that have been planned for the two purposes of raising standards in the province, not to anything like the level in the rest of Canada but to raise them to some degree, and also of providing employment, which is going to be so badly needed during the coming winter, are going to be denied to the people of Newfoundland.
We all remember-it has been referred to a good many times in the house-the statement made by the Prime Minister in Charlottetown last February a statement he made everywhere else also, that no one was going to be allowed to suffer because of unemployment. If we do not make these payments available to the government and people of Newfoundland in this session of parliament, we in this parliament are going to be creating unemployment in Newfoundland next winter. There is just no escaping that. The facts are there for anyone to see.
It is for that reason that I make no apology for joining with the premier and the leader of the opposition in Newfoundland in making this appeal to the government to act now in conformity with the unanimous request of the house of assembly of Newfoundland, supported by the Liberal majority and the Conservative minority in that assembly who have

joined together because they put the interests of Newfoundland above any partisan consideration. I may say that I am seeking to make this appeal in a completely non-controversial way in the hope that it will be received by the government in the same way and that action will be taken so that a provision may be included in the appropriation act which we will pass at the end of this session to carry out this solemn constitutional obligation to which the people of Canada gave their word on the eleventh of December, 1948, when the terms of union were signed. I think it is true to say that in the history of the modern world there has been no happier union of peoples anywhere than the union between Canada and Newfoundland.
I well remember how moved I was when sitting in the gallery on one of the anniversaries of confederation I heard the hon. member for St. John's West, the minister for Newfoundland, when he was in the first parliament after confederation, use words not dissimilar from those I have now uttered. The minister, we know, was a sincere and genuine opponent of union, but he recognized that it had come to stay. He had come to the conclusion that it was a good thing for both of us. I hold the view, and I have never hesitated to express it, that the biggest gainer as the result of union was the rest of Canada. Nevertheless, I think Canada and Newfoundland have both gained. I do feel, that we do not want any blemish on this harmonious union by any feeling in any quarter that there is any attempt whatever to fail to carry out the agreement for the union or even to delay action in carrying out the agreement.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words in support of the appeal which the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate has made to the Minister of Finance, and to the government, to implement the recommendations of the royal commission on the economic position of Newfoundland by making an interim payment at this session. For all mainlanders confederation dates back to 1867; for Newfoundlanders confederation dates back to 1949. When confederation was being considered at that earlier date, Newfoundland decided not to join with the other provinces. There were several reasons for that, but one of the very important reasons was that Newfoundland had very small taxable resources. When consideration was being given to union with Canada in 1948, this same question was in everybody's mind: What would be the effect on provincial' revenue of union with Canada? It was well known that the main sources of revenue would be taken away from Newfoundland and would be transferred to the federal government, while at the same time the province

would be left with the responsibility for the most expensive public services such as roads, schools, hospitals, health measures and so on.
The opponents of confederation, as they did in 1867, painted a very dark picture, a picture in which they said Newfoundland would be stripped of most of its sources of revenue. Confederation would result in a heavier tax burden than prevailed at that time. This was, in essence, the same argument that had been used with great effect in 1867. Subsequently, a delegation came to Canada, after confederation, to study the federal setup and try to discover just what the impact of confederation would be on provincial revenues. They studied this question for three months, not only the members of the Newfoundland delegation, but federal cabinet ministers, departmental officials and financial experts of the Bank of Canada. After studying that question for three months they had to admit that it was impossible to foresee just what effect union with Canada would have on provincial revenues. Since it was impossible to foresee what that impact would be, term 29 was drafted and inserted into the terms of union. This term 29 made provision for a review after eight years of confederation of the financial situation in Newfoundland. It was hoped it might be possible, after looking back over the course of events during the first eight years, to see more clearly what might be needed to enable the provincial government to carry out its responsibilities in the future.
I do not believe anyone had any doubt at that time that confederation would be in the best interests of the people of Newfoundland. It might bring about an increase in prosperity. But I believe that thinking people everywhere Trad some doubts as to whether or not it would be a good thing for the government of Newfoundland. There was some doubt as to whether or not it might place the government of Newfoundland in a position where it would be financially impossible to discharge its obligations. Now, eight years have passed. Some time ago a royal commission was set up to make this review. Recently, the report of that commission was tabled in this house. I am not going to make any remarks concerning the merits of the recommendations or the basis upon which the commission arrived at their conclusions or the adequacy of their recommendations. I merely wish to point out that after reviewing the situation this royal commission did recommend some money was needed to assist the provincial government in carrying out its obligations, and that sum of money should take the form of an annual grant.
Supply-Finance
As my colleague the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has pointed out, the purpose of that grant recommended by the royal commission under term 29 was merely to continue the services at the same level as had been reached when the review was made. The provincial government knew that this would happen because term 29 was actually written into the terms of union. In preparation for that review, they put forth superhuman efforts to try to make the greatest possible improvement in our public services. Every province of Canada is striving toward the goal of improved standards of public service and improved standards of living. It is a sort of race with progress. In the early days of confederation the maritime provinces were out in front. But today, after 80 years, they are behind in that race.
Newfoundland entered that race 80 years behind the others and, therefore, we are saddled with that 80-year handicap. However, as I stated, the provincial government put forth a superhuman effort and although they made mistakes as was bound to happen they did achieve a great deal. It might be worth while to inform hon. members about some of the things that have been accomplished as a result of their efforts to extend the services in Newfoundland and compare them with the services in the maritime provinces, not compare them with the high standards of the central provinces but with the standards in the maritime provinces which, as I pointed out a few minutes ago, are still behind in the race for progress.
One of our great needs in Newfoundland is roads. Roads are more expensive to build in Newfoundland than elsewhere. It is probably twice as expensive to build roads in Newfoundland as it is to build them in any other province of Canada.

speechtext: Oh, no; in British Columbia they are three times more expensive.

speechtext:
I will accept the hon. member's statement. I do not know anything about British Columbia. However, I know that they are far more expensive to build in Newfoundland than they are in Canada as a whole, having regard to average costs. In 1949 we had only 1,600 miles of road. After nine years of effort we now have 3,200 miles of road and of that 3,200 miles of road only 120 miles are paved. Let us compare our situation with that of Nova Scotia. Nova Scotia is only about half the size of Newfoundland, with an area of 22,000 square miles compared with an area of 42,200 square miles in Newfoundland. Yet Nova Scotia has
15,000	miles of road compared with 3,200 miles in Newfoundland. New Brunswick has 13,000 miles of road compared with

Supply-Finance
3,200 miles in Newfoundland. Even little Prince Edward Island with an area of 2,000 square miles, has 3,500 miles of road of which 400 miles are paved. Yet Newfoundland, with a population of over 400,000 people, still has only 3,200 miles of road.
We have one university compared with seven universities in Nova Scotia and six universities in New Brunswick. Hospital services have been more than doubled in the nine years and yet we are perhaps only within 50 per cent of what we actually need. As a result of that, Newfoundland is at least 25 years behind the rest of the maritime provinces in the standard and requirements of their public services just as the maritime provinces themselves are perhaps 25 years behind the central provinces of Ontario and Quebec.
The money provided by this grant under the terms of union which has been recommended by the royal commission is intended to enable Newfoundland only to continue 25 years behind the maritime provinces and 50 years behind the central provinces of Canada. I mention that matter in order to emphasize the fact so that hon. members will not confuse this grant under the terms of union-I refer to term 29-with the special grant for the Atlantic provinces which, as my colleague the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate has pointed out, was intended and was granted by this parliament to improve the services.
Every province wants to improve its services. But if this money is not forthcoming, Newfoundland will be obliged to divert funds from the special grant from its original purpose intended by this parliament in order to maintain existing services, and the result of that procedure is going to be to retard progress in Newfoundland for at least two or three years. Not only will it retard progress but it will also nullify the plans of the government which were intended to cope with the unemployment situation in Newfoundland which today is double what it has been in the worst year since confederation. This term 29 and the recommendations under this term represented the final act of union. It was, as it were, the consummation of the marriage between Newfoundland and Canada. We all want that marriage to be successful. We all want it to be a happy one. However, it cannot possibly be a happy marriage unless Newfoundland is given the same consideration as that given to the other provinces. If Newfoundland is prevented by any action of this government from using the special grant to improve services, as the other maritime provinces are doing, then we shall fall still further behind the other

maritime provinces in our efforts to strive for better standards of services for our people.
Nothing should be done, Mr. Chairman, by this parliament that is going to impede Newfoundland in its efforts towards progress. The government of Newfoundland, on being made aware that the special grants would be made available, worked out a program of improved services including better schools. Some of that money was also to be spent for hospitals and a great deal of it on roads. One of the roads I hoped would go to my own riding, which would open up a rich area, perhaps the only area of development in my riding in bay D'Espoir and connect it with the trans-Canada highway. These projects would create a large amount of employment and would do a great deal to stabilize the economy of Newfoundland and to minimize the effects of the recession which we are experiencing at this time. If that cannot be done, then everybody in Newfoundland is going to suffer.
I appeal to the government to give urgent consideration to our people not only because we are making the plea but because it is the right thing to do. I believe that is the only good reason for doing anything: we must be sure that it is right. I am sure that the minister and the Prime Minister want to do the right thing by Newfoundland. Withholding this grant at this time will, in my opinion-and I am sure my opinion can be substantiated by consultation with any expert on Newfoundland-strike a blow at the economy of Newfoundland from which it will take years to recover; and even if the grant were doubled next year or in some year in the future, it would still be impossible to undo or to repair the damage which will result if some interim grant is not made at this time.
The provincial government made its plans on the basis of this grant being made available for 1957. We are now into the fiscal year of 1958. It is therefore a year behind. Whatever conclusion the Prime Minister and the cabinet may reach as to the adequacy or inadequacy of these recommendations of the royal commission, I do not think that consideration should prejudice Newfoundland's right to receive interim payments on account for the last fiscal year and for this current fiscal year. I urge the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance to take our appeal seriously and to accede to the requests which they have received from the premier of Newfoundland and from the leader of the Conservative party in Newfoundland which show that this is a matter which is far above party politics and party division. I am sure there is no better way

in which to ensure the gratitude of Newfoundland than by taking this most needed action at this time.

I would like to say a few words at this time in support of the appeal made by my colleague, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and also by my colleague, the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo. There is at this time very little need to recount the proceedings leading up to the joining of Newfoundland with Canada. I suspect the story is well known and those who have read the official record in Hansard will be fully informed of what took place at that time. The Hon. George Drew, who was then leader of the Conservative party, on Monday, February 7, 1949, had the following to say:
As has already been pointed out by the Prime Minister, the union of Newfoundland with Canada will represent the fulfilment of the great and challenging vision of those who met in Charlottetown on September 1, 1864, in the hope of bringing together the whole of British North America as one united nation. It will give reality to the dream Df Sir John A. Macdonald, whose proposals to Newfoundland for confederation were not first made at the time of the Charlottetown conference but in fact were put forward to Newfoundland in 1858. It is well to remember the significance of the fact that these proposals which were put forward to Newfoundland in 1858 brought the first favourable official response to his contention that steps should then be taken to create a federal union.
Further down in his statement Mr. Drew had this to say:
Macdonald, Cartier, and those associated with them, were disappointed that Newfoundland did not become part of Canada in 1867, but they never despaired of ultimate success.
Towards the end of his speech, he had this to say:
Supply-Finance
It is essential that the union be one which appeals now, and will appeal in the years ahead, to the people of Newfoundland and to the people of Canada as something which united them in spirit and in friendship even more than it did in statutory form.
It was only two months following the statement of the Hon. Mr. Drew that Newfoundland did become part of Canada and as part of Canada there were naturally terms of union between us. I know that term No. 29 has already been placed on the record, but I want to repeat part of it again as follows:
In view of the difficulty of predicting with sufficient accuracy the financial consequences to Newfoundland of becoming a province of Canada, the government of Canada will appoint a royal commission within eight years from date of union to review the financial position of the province of Newfoundland and to recommend the form and scale of additional financial assistance, if any, that may be required by the government of the province of Newfoundland to enable it to continue public services at the levels and standards-
I repeat that, Mr. Chairman-
-at the levels and standards reached subsequent to the date of union, without resorting to taxation more burdensome, having regard to capacity to pay, than obtaining generally in the region comprising the maritime provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Prince Edward Island.
Obviously at the time these terms of union were signed it was impossible to look ahead to see what the effect of the terms of union would be on the province of Newfoundland and so, included in these terms of union was term 29 by which, after eight years, it would be possible with the help of experience in intervening years to look back on what had been done and to see how these terms of union had affected Newfoundland and what, if any, additional consideration should be given.
We know that in Newfoundland we have standards of public service which are not nearly up to the level of the standards here on the mainland. I could refer to many instances but I will just briefly mention two of them. Take, for example, our educational services, which are not nearly as good as that enjoyed by the people in any other Canadian province. We have a growing population with a great need for school expansion including those modern educational services which are being given in many places to the people of Canada.
I heard my hon. friend from Victoria, B.C., make an interjection when my colleague from Burin-Burgeo was speaking regarding the cost of highways. He may be perfectly correct in that the cost of the trans-Canada highway being built in British Columbia is much higher than it would be in Newfoundland but of course when you start to calculate the cost of that highway in any province I think you

Supply-Finance
must consider not only the cost in dollars and cents per mile but the actual cost in dollars and cents per capita.
Earlier in the session I put some figures on the record which I would like to quote again. At page 409 of Hansard for May 23, 1958, I said:
I point out that the project is becoming a very expensive one for my province, not only in the sense that Newfoundland is not an easy province in which to build a highway, but it is expensive also in terms of the amount of road which has to be built by a small population. The total length of the trans-Canada highway is about 4,500 miles. The total length of that highway in Newfoundland is 610 miles, which means that while the population of Newfoundland is only 3.7 per cent of the population of all the provinces which are now under the agreement, yet the proportion of the road which they have to build is 13.3 per cent, roughly three times as much.
We could compare the cost of the trans-Canada highway in Newfoundland with the cost in other provinces, for example in Alberta and in Ontario, where the number of miles per 10,000 of population is 2.8. In Manitoba the number of miles per 10,000 population is 3.7. In Saskatchewan the figure is 4.8 miles, in Nova Scotia 4.8, in British Columbia 5.7, in New Brunswick 7.1, in Prince Edward Island 7.3, while in Newfoundland the number of miles per 10,000 of population is 15.8.
I suggest to my hon. friend that while the actual cost per mile may be greater in British Columbia, the actual cost per capita in Newfoundland is far greater than in any other province of Canada. I could go on to talk about other services in Newfoundland and indicate that we still have a long way to go not only to reach the standards and levels of the maritime provinces but also to reach the standards and levels that obtain in the other provinces of Canada.
I could, of course, engage in a long speech and quote figures at length from the McNair report and also from the various briefs presented to that royal commission dealing with the situation that exists in Newfoundland but I shall not do so.
We live in a country that is known as a democratic country. We live in a country that is recognized for its practice of democracy. Democracy is, after all, an experiment in faith. It is an experiment in the faith that free men are able to retain their identity and maintain the fact that there is such a thing as unity in multiplicity. Perhaps the concept that there can be unity in multiplicity is the very basis of democracy. After all, the confederation of Canada in 1867 is a fact that goes to attest these ideas. It demonstrates that in a large country with many provinces covering a wide expanse those provinces have been able to unite to form one great nation. In 1949 Newfoundland entered that union and in doing so they, too, as an older dominion in their own right believed that there is such a thing as unity

in multiplicity. Those who come from the province of British Columbia are proud that they come from that great province but I suggest to you that they are also proud because they are Canadians. We could go right across the country from Alberta to Prince Edward Island and in every province it will be found that people are proud to belong to their own province but at the same time are proud to be Canadians.
We in Newfoundland never hope to have the industrial development that exists in British Columbia. Newfoundland can never hope to be a Toronto or a Montreal. Yet, we do believe that we can be an integral part of this nation. We believe that with our God-fearing people who are resolute and determined we can make a significant contribution to this nation. We in Newfoundland are proud to be Newfoundlanders and I believe if this government gives to Newfoundland the assistance the people there deserve they in turn will be proud to be Canadians. I urge the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance, the cabinet and hon. gentlemen of this committee to give serious consideration to the appeal made by the premier of Newfoundland, by the leader of the opposition and by the hon. members from Newfoundland here in the House of Commons on behalf of Newfoundland, for I assure you, gentlemen, that if we can give to Newfoundland the start that it deserves it will become a fine part of this country, and the loyalty to Canada on the part of the people of Newfoundland, if it is excelled in the future, will be excelled only by those who have always had the privilege of calling themselves Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened with great interest this evening to the remarks made by hon. members from the province of Newfoundland and those made by my colleague the hon. member for Kootenay West. I am not well acquainted with this question but I know sufficient about it to wonder why the government has failed to act in a way that would remove this important and justifiable complaint of the province of Newfoundland.
If the discussion had nothing to do with the terms of confederation, and that is far from the case, I think hon. members would be justified in asking such consideration from the federal treasury to help them improve their health services, their roads and educational services in that province. But it is clear from the terms of confederation that within eight years from the date of union, in April, 1949, there should be consideration by the government to providing to Newfoundland such revenues as are necessary to maintain the services prevalent at that time

with a tax burden not greater than that borne by the citizens of the neighouring maritime provinces.
We have heard a great deal about national unity in this country. When the Liberal party was in power it heralded itself as the party of national unity and it was the Conservative opposition at that time, according to the Liberal members, who were bent on damaging national unity in this country. Up until this moment during this session we have seen the government take upon itself the cloak of the supporters of national unity and hon. members of the government have accused the opposition of not following policies in the interests of national unity when they were in power.
I believe if we can leave our politics aside hon. gentlemen in all parties would be found to be interested in maintaining and strengthening national unity. I believe that hon. members of this committee have great sympathy for the position being taken by the province of Newfoundland. That position is a very strong one stemming as it does from the unanimous report of the royal commission and the unanimous resolution passed by the Newfoundland house of assembly. This parliament should not allow this problem to go unsolved, should not allow this criticism to gain strength and should not permit to exist a disservice to national unity in Canada.
I have been called a lot of things in this house but I had never before been called a mainlander as I was tonight by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo. However, I want to assure him that as one mainlander I have every sympathy for the problem put forward by the province of Newfoundland. I believe the province has an excellent and unanswerable case and that the parliament of this nation should fulfil in a generous way beyond question the terms of confederation with Newfoundland to the very letter and spirit of the agreement and if necessary should go beyond the terms of the agreement to make sure that the Canadian citizens living in the province of Newfoundland without exception are proud to be a part of this great nation.

I wish to state that this is not a case of a have-not province looking for more money from Ottawa. It is also more than the mere fulfilment of a contractual obligation to be considered in the light of a transaction in the market place. It is rather the completion of a compact which brought two peoples together in an indissoluble union, and the success of that union depends on mutual satisfaction and, in respect of the weaker party to the union, upon their ability to find respect and happiness within the orbit of a great and growing nation.
Let me assure this committee, Mr. Chairman, with all the sincerity I can muster that Newfoundland's future as a province of Canada depends in a large measure on the action taken on this report. For some time we have heard much about this report and I assure you, Mr. Chairman, that Newfoundlanders had hopes that the cabinet would have given serious consideration to the McNair report and would have dealt with it swiftly because of its importance to Newfoundland.
Let me say as well that I had hoped as a Newfoundlander that this question of the revision of the financial term of union would be dealt with on a level that goes beyond party politics, or even the regional or provincial issues and differences that sometimes tend to keep us apart. I believe sincerely that it would be a real tragedy if the future of a great new province were to become the subject of petty haggling or even party politics. I hasten to add that I have not the slightest suggestion that this will be the case. Indeed, I have every reason to believe that the Prime Minister, his associates in the cabinet and indeed all members on both sides of this house have a high regard for Newfoundland. It is apparent that the vast majority of Canadians, both public men and private citizens, wish to see Newfoundlanders take their places as prosperous citizens in a prosperous province, sharing equally in all the undoubted benefits of Canadian citizenship.
It merely remains for me to assure this committee in all sincerity that the feeling is mutual. What Newfoundland seeks from this union is not charity. A people with more than 450 years of history behind them are much too proud for that. What we want is common justice and an opportunity to pull our weight as we have done in all cases in the past. It is not surprising, indeed it is understandable, that hon. members and all Canadians in general have little real knowledge of its people. After all, nine years of confederation is a relatively short period in which to educate a whole nation to the attributes of a neighbour and partner, particularly in view of the fact that the education job has to be done in the face of a previous century or

Supply-Finance
more of false impressions and erroneous information. Obviously, in a single speech it is going to be impossible for me to correct all the current misconceptions which even this committee may share.
I do suggest to this committee, however, that as public men it would serve us well if we were to devote some time to a study of our newest province. I believe you will find its history fascinating and its people admirable. You might learn, as I did long ago, that while the problems of Newfoundland may seem gigantic by some yardsticks, our people do not in fact require a great deal more to make them self-sufficient and give them a happy life. Newfoundland today has a desperate, almost hopeless effort to catch up with the rest of Canada. Remember that virtually all of the remainder of the nation had at least 50 years of confederation behind it before Newfoundland entered the union, and thus from that moment on, although the pact was share and share alike, it is difficult to see how Newfoundland could hope to be anything but a half century behind in its basic services.
Let me put it this way. If I entered into a partnership with a member of this house and he had $50,000 at that time while I did not have a cent, and if we accepted the fact that we would share everything equally from that point on, it stands to reason that my so-called partner would always be $50,000 better off than I. That is precisely the position of Newfoundland relative to other provinces. We got the same deal as other provinces on the trans-Canada highway but our existing roads mileage was very low and below that of other areas of this country.
We get the same federal grants, the same rental programs and the same treatment generally, but we have so much farther to come in order to achieve equality that we never can hope to catch up under such an agreement. Newfoundland needs and is to have special aid, and there is a good case to be made for such an agreement. It is a case that needs no appeal to charity or unusual generosity. Rather, it is based on logic and above all justice. It is very true that Canada has given much to Newfoundland in the past nine years and I think that union has been a good thing for the vast majority of Newfoundlanders but it is equally true, although not as widely publicized that Newfoundland has given much to Canada.
Not all of this contribution can be measured in dollars and cents, although from the financial point of view the Newfoundland role has been substantial. However, perhaps

the intangibles have been even more important. Over 400,000 good citizens, a practically debt-free people, assume the responsibility for their share of Canada's debt; the world's greatest fishing grounds, strategic defence bases, airports, water power and a strong hand in dealing with the United States. All this plus much more came to Canada through its union with Newfoundland, making the union truly a two-way street of mutual benefit. Given a fair measure of the nation's wealth, Newfoundland has a bright and promising future.
Newfoundland is not greatly different from other parts of Canada and its people are pretty much like those from other constituencies. We ask nothing more than the right to earn a decent living, through our own efforts, and to enjoy for ourselves and our families that degree of basic security that has come to be regarded as our right in a nation that has not forgotten the worth of the individual.
Therefore it is on this basis that I say and believe Newfoundland should have the support of the house in seeing that a good and just case exists for an upward revision of the terms of union and that, according to the report of the royal commission, Newfoundland finances are raised to a higher level.

Your attention has no doubt been drawn to statements by myself and the leader of the opposition in our assembly respecting the inadequate nature of the recommendations of the royal commission on the revision of term 29 of the terms of union of Canada and Newfoundland. We plan to use our share of the Atlantic provinces grant largely for employment creating improvements in our public services. They also urgently needed the amount recommended by the commission, and needed it now for the reasons the premier sets out here, for the welfare of the province, for the maintenance of employment, for the maintenance of essential services. This is what is being denied them and being denied in spite of this unanimous appeal from the assembly, an appeal from the premier and the leader of the opposition, the leader of the Conservative party in the province. They should be allowed, like the rest of the provinces, to use it to improve services. In so far as the Atlantic provinces grant is concerned, what the Prime Minister was saying in his reply was that, while Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick could use the Atlantic provinces grant to improve their services, Newfoundland has to use it to maintain existing services. The statement by the Prime Minister that they would receive more under these two payments than they would under this award is, in fact, not correct. I do not accuse the Prime Minister of any deliberate intent, but in fact so far as this particular year is concerned, that is not correct. Invariably the Indian fishermen of whom I know who want to buy gill netters or to build a gill net boat and who need money for this purpose find that the only place where they might be able to get financial assistance is the fishing company for whom they may be working. This is a most unfortunate state of affairs, as the minister probably knows, for once a person becomes indebted to a particular company, especially if that person is a fisherman, it is most difficult to get away from the clutches of that company. There are many details of the act which require to be changed but I think one of the most important things in so far as native Indians are concerned is a revision in order that Indians may be able to borrow money under the act, if not from a bank then from a credit union; if not from a private source then through some treasury source.
I hope the minister will take this matter into consideration and will study the act to see whether or not it is possible to amend it so that native Indians will have a better opportunity to themselves finance their purchases and reconstruction of boats.

127. To authorize payments to the national conference of Canadian universities in accordance with the agreement entered into between the conference and the Minister of Finance on the 26th day of March, 1957, pursuant to vote 541, Appropriation Act No. 1, 1957, $17,100,000.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on this vitally important item, I think that, in view of the stand taken by the province of Quebec, we should pause for a few moments to consider this matter of assistance to education, this assistance to universities.
We know that, in 1951, the Liberal party instituted a policy of assistance to universities by granting an average of 50 cents per capita and that it subsequently increased that grant. As early as 1951, there was unanimous agreement in this house on this subject. Indeed, we can see what the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) said at the time, by referring to page 5021 of Hansard. I quote:
(Text):
I commend the Prime Minister and the government for the speed with which they have dealt with this matter.

Supply-Finance
(Translation):
And here is what the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) had to say, as found on page 2633 of Hansard for 1951: (Text):
-that the Prime Minister aroused high hopes on the part of Canadian universities.
(Translation):
And now, this is what Mr. Solon Low had to say, as found on page 4279 of Hansard for 1951:
(Text):
I say that we are very happy that the government is taking this step now to provide some form of interim assistance to the universities.
(Translation):
As can be seen from page 4279 for Hansard for 1951, the then member for Saskatoon, Mr. Knight, who had always advocated aid to universities, stated that this was a matter of prime concern to him and hastened to thank the Prime Minister for the good news.
This indicates that, in 1951, there seemed to be general unanimity among the parties represented in this house with regard to increased aid for universities. In 1957 the universities were still in such a position that the government of the day felt it had to do more and to grant a further increase of 50c.
There has been talk of urgency in respect of this matter. Here is what Mr. St. Laurent had to say on the subject. Before introducing this legislation he had stated, in a lecture delivered at the University of Toronto, and this is reproduced in Hansard for 1951, page 2633:
(Text):
I think many of us recognize increasingly that some means must be found to ensure our universities the financial capacity to perform the many services which are required in the interest of the whole nation.
(Translation):
In 1957, I note that the present Prime Minister himself made a rather significant statement which can be found on page 400 of Hansard, volume I. He said at the time:
I mentioned the need of Canadian universities. The need is becoming greater as the days go by. A survey was recently made to ascertain the degree to which universities in other parts of the world are dependent on grants from the state. In Great Britain 73.6 per cent of college income is from government grants. In the United States it is 58.6 per cent, and in Canada it is 42 per cent. More and more young and worthy students are being denied admission to university because they are unable to meet the ever-rising costs of tuition. In Canadian universities, of the total income today, or until the recent increase announced by the Prime Minister in November, 30 per cent comes from student fees. In the United Kingdom it is 10.7 per cent and in the United States it is 21.4 per cent. Unless action is taken to meet that situation it cannot but result in many outstanding and potential

leaders in the sciences, in the arts, and in all the different phases of living, being denied an education; for more and more tuition rates are being raised and worthy students are finding greater and greater difficulty in proceeding to senior education.
At a national conference held in November 1956 in Ottawa on the crisis in the field of higher education in Canada, the representatives of Canadian universities, in a resolution passed unanimously, expressed:
The well-considered opinion that it was their urgent responsibility to warn Canadians that the problem of universities has become a critical issue of national importance which certainly hinders our development and our status as a nation, and that this problem can only be solved by the active and immediate assistance and co-operation of all government levels in Canada, with business, industry and private benefactors.
On May 10, 1951, Mr. Cyril James, vicechancellor and principal of McGill University said, according to a report published in the Globe and Mail:
(Text):
A university education costs Canadian students more than in other countries.
A young Canadian from a family of modest circumstances has less chance of getting a university education today than a youth in any other country with which I am familiar.
He urged government to participate in the cost of education because work of the universities was of vital importance to the community, and government has not lived up to this responsibility in Canada during the last two decades, as far as education of civilians was concerned.
(Translation):
Mr. George Drew said this, which is found on page 4278 of Hansard of 1951:
(Text):
I am sure hon. members generally will welcome any measure of assistance given in this way to the universities of Canada.
(Translation):
The word "generally" referred no doubt to a very limited number of members, such as the then member for Labelle, now Secretary of State (Mr. Courtemanche), who was more interested in politics than in the welfare of students and their families, and of institutions of higher learning.
The present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) said, as recorded on page 488 of Hansard of February 19, 1951:
(Text):
I would like to say, however, that last year the resolution seemed to receive support from practically everyone who spoke, on all sides of the house. The same thing appears to be true today, so it would seem to me the time has now come to put an end to talk on the matter and let us have some action toward implementing it.

(Translation):
The Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Brooks) said also, as recorded on pages 484 and 485 of Hansard of February 19, 1951:
(Text):
I feel that some responsibility for education must be borne by the federal government, and I could give many reasons. One of the chief reasons is that the small provinces cannot today afford to give to their people the educational facilities to which they are entitled, or that they should have. ... I am in wholehearted support of the resolution and I hope that for the interest of Canada and for the people as a whole, from one end of the country to the other, some means may be found whereby educational opportunities may equal to all people from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
(Translation) :
I note that the hon. Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) said on December 1, 1953, as recorded on pages 506 to 509 of Hansard:
(Text):
What are they going to do about the problems that are facing universities in this country? Something must be done to maintain their strength, to enable them to develop, to enable them to go forward. In these days, owing to indirect action of the government, the high level of taxation and succession duties, universities are deprived of those moneys and private beneficence which at one time they used to get. I say it is the responsibility of the government to come to their assistance, and this is a reasonable proposition that is advanced by the presidents at the conference of universities.
(Translation):
I note on page 254 of Hansard of 1955 the following statement of the same minister:
The problem has increased alarmingly in the last few years. It is a problem, of course, which I am sure the government will have to look at in a far wider field within the next five to ten years, because we are just on the verge of a new problem with respect to universities.
He no doubt referred to the problem resulting from the increasing birth-rate and the large number of immigrants arriving in Canada.
And the same minister is reported as saying on page 5345 of Hansard, 1956:
Practically every university in the maritime provinces with the exception of one, is financed by private charity or by endowment.
For his part, Dr. Blair is reported as saying on page 5079 of Hansard, 1956, in questioning Mr. Gillis:
Is he aware that the universities have had to increase their fees and that some of the universities are running these courses at a loss? They are practically all running them at a loss. The hon. member made the statement they were in business. I cannot agree with that. They are not in business, and they are running these courses at a loss.
Mr. Low is reported as saying, on page 3401 of Hansard, 1956:
Supply-Finance
Yes, in another ten or twelve years the universities are going to be in exactly the same position. In fact, they are feeling the impact right now. Certainly we should look forward and make provision ahead of time for these heavy burdens that will have to be carried.
As for the member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue)-the present house party leader of the C.C.F., reference to page 346 of Hansard, 1955, will show that he complained that the prime minister yielded to the Quebec premier's strait-jacketed nationalism to the extent of denying education to the other provinces.
As you can see, Mr. Chairman, sympathy is manifested on this matter by both sides of the house.
Furthermore, Monseigneur Lussier, rector of the University of Montreal, said that if a final solution was not found to the university problem, the universities would become bankrupt.
Those are the remarks of people of experience, people with a university background who appreciate what is done by the universities.
I state then that the government can be congratulated on having provided a further increase of 50 cents in university grants. This is a matter of prime importance.
To those who seem to feel that we in the province of Quebec who form the largest minority in Canada should stand apart from the others, I will say that in every country where there is a minority it is absolutely essential that that minority be intellectually superior to the majority to become equal to it in other fields. That is why we should consider that matter, not in so far as it concerns our own personal future but in so far as it involves that of generations yet to come.
The constitutional issue has been raised. On this point we all agree that section 93 of the constitution is clear and unequivocal and that it does vest the provinces with exclusive jurisdiction in the field of education.
What is the field of education? Does it mean putting up buildings? Does it mean scholarships awarded for supplementary studies? I believe that the "exclusive right in relation to education" means that the province, alone, shall exercise supervision. That is it: to supervise so that the subjects taught be in accordance with the needs of the province. There, in my mind, lies the problem. And as long as provinces maintain their authority with respect to the working out of school curricula, no constitutional problem can be said to exist. The mere fact of granting sums of money to facilitate the building of schools does not mean encroachment on the field of education and is not contrary to the spirit of section 93 of the British North America Act.
