Supply-Finance
And besides, in that field-
Mr. Chairman, every time we say anything to the point, I see that the hon. member tor Roberval (Mr. Tremblay) shakes with laughter, thus displaying the value of his culture.
The Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer) said, page 273 of Hansard for 1952. I apologize, but I have only the English version and could not find the other version.
(Text):
For instance, let us consider education. Education is the exclusive field of the provinces, granted to them by the British North America Act. While every province has always kept a jealous watch over its autonomy in the field of education, we, in the province of Quebec realize that it is the very foundation of our racial and religious survival,-
(Translation),:
And the hon. member for Three Rivers continued:
(Text):
-and the population of the province of Quebec will never give up on that point. No doubt the federal government, with its millions in surpluses, will put forward very tempting offers of direct subsidies. They should know, though, as the leader of the opposition so well put it, that what the provinces need in this connection are not horse traders' gifts, but merely the respect of those ideas which served to inspire the fathers of confederation.
(Translation):
And, at pages 2543 and 2547 of Hansard for 1952-1953, the hon. member for Three Rivers said that education must be left entirely to the provinces; here is what that same member stated on another occasion that same year, at page 762 of Hansard:
(Text) :
Mr. Chairman, like all other hon. members who have spoken on this subject, I am greatly alarmed by the difficult situation which the Canadian universities are in at the present time. Like all other hon. members in this house I have the greatest respect for my own alma mater, namely Laval University. I can easily picture all the problems that face this great institution at the present time, having regard to the increase in the cost of living, the increase in the cost of materials, and various other difficulties which the authorities of this great university must face at the present time. However, I am sorry to be the only voice so far which has been raised against this vote.
(Translation):
Therefore, the hon. member for Three Rivers, when he sat in the opposition, was opposed to the payment of grants to universities on the ground that such grants are unconstitutional and a violation of section 93 of the constitution of Canada. Later on, the hon. member for Three Rivers said-I quote from page 770 of Hansard for 1957:
Mr. Chairman, before recess I was stating my opposition to this item although, like other members of the house, I recognize the difficulties faced by Canadian universities. Quebec universities face

such difficulties as do those of other provinces, and provincial governments have to make great efforts to help them.
However, he stated that he was going to vote but that he could not approve the appropriation for assistance to the universities in the 1957 estimates.
And according to the official record of 1951 -p.p. 905 to 908-the Secretary of State (Mr. Courtemanche), said the following:
(Text):
Better known as the Massey commission, it (the royal commission on national development on the arts, letters and sciences in Canada) could more accurately and more realistically be described as the royal commission for the promotion of centralization in Canada. There is no point in trying to hide the truth: the investigation in itself was a breach of provincial autonomy, as are also the attempts to implement various recommendations inconsistent with our constitution, incompatible with the sovereigny of the provinces.
(Translation):
There again in the same speech, the hon. member for Labelle objected and categorically refused to vote in favour of estimates earmarked for assistance to universities, with the excuse that such action would be unconstitutional, and in this, being in the opposition, he was going against the wishes of his then leader, Mr. Drew.
Yet, on the same constitutional issue, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith), who was then president of the University of Toronto had this to say:
(Text):
Dr. Sydney Smith, then president of Toronto University, is reported in the Globe and Mail of May 7, 1951, as follows:
He noted that it cost the university $1,000 a year to keep one student in an art course. Yet the student pays a fee of $240.
Answering any argument that education is a provincial matter and therefore the federal government should keep out of it, he produced statistics which showed that 20 per cent of the 100,000 living alumni of the University of Toronto are in other provinces. The university is therefore making a national contribution. The same is true of all other Canadian universities.
(Translation):
Now, I should like to refer to the testimony of Mr. Cyril James, and I quote from page 512 of the 1953-54 session:
On the question of provincial rights, the brief said flatly: "There is no control of education, no infringement of provincial autonomy in the grants."
It said that: "Neither the members of parliament who voted unanimously for the grant, nor the universities of Canada which were equally unanimous in accepting it, entertained the remotest idea that the federal grant carried any implications of control."
The possibility of any future danger to provincial rights is obviated by the presence of a provincial representative on the joint federal-provincial commission which administers the grants, it added.
Then, further on we find this:

Dr. James said the land grant to Manitoba university was cited "because many men who participated in the confederation discussions were still active at that time."
And further:
..."it has never been suggested that in making such gifts the donors were legislating with respect to education"...
Similarly, while the Quebec government cannot legislate with regard to education in France, it nonetheless contributes generously to the Canadian students' house in Paris "and provides equally generous scholarships for students wishing to study in French universities."
And still further:
"It is difficult to see how the legality of such federal grants can be questioned without similarly calling into question a wide variety of governmental practices, provincial as well as federal, which have been part of our accepted tradition for many years."
Mr. Cyril James is an expert in the field of education, a man whose opinions generally carry much weight and I think he spelled out the problem as it should be when he said that no control in matters of curricula was implied. Moreover, he pointed out that the province of Quebec granted scholarships to students for studies in Paris, while at the same time giving assistance to the student house in Paris.
The Quebec government has done all that, and it claims that other governments do not have the right to intervene by offering grants to the provincial government itself, and I remember commending it for grants made to the university of Ottawa, to the St. Boniface college in Manitoba as well as to a college in the maritimes. This was excellent. I do not feel that in doing so he recognized that he was under any obligation to ask the Manitoba government, or the Ontario government or the various provincial governments in the maritime provinces for permission to grant subsidies or grants in aid to education.
Indeed, the present Prime Minister himself said on page 648 of Hansard for 1952 and I will quote only briefly:
(Text):
Simply paraphrasing a slogan of another day, the attitude of this party is: federal assistance ever, federal supervision never. That sums up our attitude on this matter.
(Translation):
That is why I am not in the least surprised to note that the present government has seen fit to increase those grants, in the face of ever increasing difficulties. In fact, the present Minister of Trade and Commerce stated, as will be seen on page 632 of Hansard for 1952:
(Text):
The answer lies in adequate financial support for education, with the federal authority providing the additional assistance that the provinces require- The provinces, unless blessed with unusual natural
57071-3-293J
Supply-Finance
resources, are unable to maintain from their restricted fields of direct taxation the services required. Some people consider that federal support for education means inevitably federal control or interference. Ottawa should not be allowed to grip any part of the provincial educational system. Education is of national concern and merits support from the federal treasury. Education is not just one among many competing welfare services. It is basic to the development of a democratic society. Education is a right which should not be denied any child in Canada. Opportunity for higher education should be the privilege of every Canadian boy and girl.
(Translation):
And the minister concluded with these words:
(Text):
Present interest by the federal authorities can be increased and present federal aid to education can be enlarged without curtailing provincial jurisdiction and responsibility.
(Translation):
And the same minister also said, as will be seen in Hansard for the same year, page 632:
(Text):
The federal government has established a pattern of assistance without control and is showing an interest in education. Education is of national concern and merits support from the federal treasury.
(Translation):
Further, on page 625 of Hansard for 1952, we can read the following remarks made by the present Minister of Transport:
(Text):
Now, I believe that the federal government should make funds available on a sliding scale to help equalize the opportunity for education between the provinces ... It would not be my intention that the federal government should take any part in the policy or administration of education. This field belongs to the provinces alone.
(Translation):
In the same debate the Minister of Veterans Affairs stated:
(Text):
I do not think for one moment that the federal government could or would interfere with laws made by the provinces concerning education. It is my belief, however, that this provision in the British North America Act is concerned chiefly with the curriculum and administration of the schools. We can still give financial aid and in no way interfere with the administration of the laws of the provinces.
(Translation):
Mr. George Drew also said, as can be seen on page 584 of the official record of the house for 1951:
(Text):
I would point out, however, that ways have been found of assisting in different fields, including the field of education, without in any way interfering with the division of constitutional responsibility.

Supply-Finance
(Translation):
I will refrain from giving other quotations because I see that my time is running out. Indeed, I could quote several people who expressed the opinion that the federal government should step in the field of education because provinces cannot alone bear the whole cost of it. All levels of government and business institutions should get together in order to give assistance.
In fact, I note the following remarks made by Mr. Knight, as taken from page 3445 of Hansard for 1956:
I know that education is a matter of provincial jurisdiction. X agree completely with that view so far as administration and curricula are concerned.
And that is the important point because, when the curricula are protected by the provinces, the federal government may intervene, give grants and even increase them, without encroaching on the field of education.
Mr. Maurice Breton, former member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, had this to say, as taken from page 394 of Hansard for 1953-54:
Education is what we are interested in. Let us consider the matter. Evidently, under section 93, the federal government could not set up a system of education in the province of Quebec or in any other province: it could neither create boards of education nor establish school curricula. All such things come strictly under provincial jurisdiction.
But does the wording as written mean explicitly that the federal government is not authorized to intervene, even in the interest of public order and good administration of the country, and give, without restrictions and unconditionally, to a public body in need the necessary grants to enable it to attain the purpose for which it was set up?
Mr. Chairman, I see that I have nearly run out of time and I hear some hon. members- (Text):

I said a few minutes. I know that the hon. member who has just interrupted me could not deal with that subject for more than two minutes owing to his state of mind but I have a lot more to say.

Mr. Chairman, we know that it is not the first time that the federal government has given assistance in the field of education. In fact, in 1913, the federal government, led by Sir Robert Borden granted a sum of $10 million for agricultural schools. In 1919, under the government of Sir Robert Borden, a sum of $10 million was voted to help technical schools. In 1939, the government led by the Right Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King granted a sum of $4,500,000 to help our youth.
In 1952 the Liberal administration approved a grant of $51 million under the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act.
In 1951 the federal government made $7,500,000 available through a grant in aid to universities.
As you will note, these subsidies are by no means new. This is no recent policy. Indeed, we have seen that this has obtained for a considerable time.
Referring to the people of Quebec the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) made a few remarks which I felt I had to contradict in some respects but which were, in fact, quite true in others. These may be found on page 121 of Hansard for 1955:
The people of Quebec are suffering. They are subjected to double taxation and they are not enjoying the facilities in the field of education which they would like to have, which they ought to have and which they deserve as Canadian citizens.
In support of his arguments, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam referred to the survey that Mr. Enfield, then Liberal member for York-Scarborough, recorded in Hansard, on January 10, 1957, in connection with the total aid which the various federal departments had given to the provinces in the field of education. A study of that survey indicates that in 1955-56 the province of Ontario received $7,228,000, while the province of Quebec received only $2,952,000, which represents an enormous difference as compared to the other provinces. Actually, Quebec cannot afford to refuse the subsidies, because the population there is in need of education which the province is unable to provide.
I shall now refer to some excerpts of another survey recorded in Hansard by Mr. Knight, which indicates that in the province of Quebec, the cost of elementary and high school amounts to $139.48 per pupil, while in Ontario it amounts to $190.82.
The same survey shows that there were 1643 unqualified teachers because the school boards could not afford to pay higher salaries. That survey also showed that among pupils reaching grade 11, 9.4 per cent only are French-Canadian Catholics, while

41.8 per cent are Protestants, which shows that the situation that prevailed in 1947 has not changed very much.
It must be realized that it costs a man $1,300 a year, if he does not live in a university town, to send his son to the university. If we take the case of a father of five or six children, earning between $4,000 and $5,000 a year, how will he manage to give all his children the education which will permit them to fully develop their ability? He will have to ask certain members of his family to make enormous sacrifices so that the others may carry on their studies. Is it fair to ask a father in the province of Quebec for such a sacrifice when it is not requested of the head of a family in other provinces?
Grants where given to a provincial government should necessarily be subject to certain conditions. If the grants were made by the federal government, let us stop our fruitless fights, because we are losing precious material. Human values are being sacrificed to small party politics.
We must educate our men. They will then know how to defend the real rights of provinces and minorities. Let us eliminate true or false ignorance-and I am addressing myself more particularly to the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Tremblay)-and the threats of extinction will forever disappear, when we create enough men of good will to ensure mutual understanding. Only at such time will we be able to speak of a Canadian nation united in its diversity.
Mr. Chairman, I will conclude on this note. We are at this time concerned with an item which we are asked to approve by the Minister of Finance. I support that item, knowing as I do that our universities and educational institutions need assistance. They require that increased assistance which the federal government has just introduced. However there are some gentlemen who, during the last general election, in the province of Quebec, were quite content to leave the universities to struggle with their difficulties and preferred to see their own fellow citizens grow in ignorance rather than accept those measures of relief which would allow them to get ahead in the intellectual field. I was just wondering how they were going to vote on this measure.
There is talk of disappearance of race and religion. However, if the race was to have disappeared, it would have happened back in 1760, at a time when there were very, very few of us, a small group of rather uneducated people. At this time, however, we make up more than one fifth of the population of this country and if we refuse these university grants, we will endanger the very life of our

province. Some day we will have to go along with the rest of Canada, as long as the federal government does not interfere with the educational program of our province. I know, Mr. Chairman, that we must reach that point some day and I therefore ask that a vote be taken immediately on that item.

speechtext:
Since there must be unanimous consent to continue, I shall rise and report progress. Tomorrow, we will be starting on vote No. 503.
Resolutions adopted in committee of supply this day reported and concurred in.

speakerposition: topic

speechtext: I wonder whether the leader of the house could tell us what the order of business will be for tomorrow. I presume the bill of rights comes first tomorrow. Can he tell us what will be the order of business afterwards?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: As I understand it, there will be speeches by the leaders of the three parties on the first reading of the bill of rights. When we get down to the orders of the day we shall commence with item No. 2-

Is it proposed to have those speeches before orders of the day are reached?

Supply-Items Passed
There is introduction of bills.
I know. But would the minister consider having orders of the day called first before the speeches?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am not in a position to say that tonight. I do not know that it makes very much difference. But according to the order paper these speeches would be made on the first reading. Then we shall take item No. 2, second reading of a bill to amend the Customs Act; item No. 3, a bill to amend the Canadian Citizenship Act; and then the completion of the estimates.
At 10.34 p.m. the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
